I graded three claims, so I cannot establish the universal; and the exception as worded covers only "C13's time-varying measurements", whereas C13's `render` pair 486 / 373271 is presented under Scope as reproducible-because-frozen and also does not range over the pinned tree — it includes `.git/` and `/target`, neither of which is tracked content at that commit.

Every independently checkable clause holds, but the claim's central universal cannot be established by this pass, exactly as its own last sentence predicts. Only C1 and C13 were owed on this schedule, so eleven of the thirteen claims were not re-read against the pinned tree by me at all; and the clause is in any case an attestation about where the author looked rather than a property of the tree. Separately worth flagging for the reader rather than against the claim: the worktree HEAD is now 5b8dd8c58f20ebdb572b08c2bb420200a60fc54f, so "that tree" is reachable only through `git show`/`git ls-tree`/`git grep` at the pin, which is how every reading here was taken.

records.prop: Every input the ticket names is present and travels with the memo: prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl ship inside `<memo>.tetel/`, each event in them carries a `timestamp: u64`, the prose→claim citation edges are the `cite` field of prose events, and a rendered ledger claim id is byte-identical to the workspace claim id. Two things the ticket does not name are also true and constrain the design: both loaders discard every timestamp, so the check must read the logs rather than the loaded types; and a prose block's own id is never written into the rendered document, so a residue line naming `P4` names something no reader of the memo alone can locate.
verdicts: Every enumerated item is witnessed: prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl are in SNAPSHOT_FILES and copied into `<memo>.tetel/` (F2); every prose and claim event carries `timestamp: u64` and the citation edge is the prose event's `cite` field (F3); both loaders drop timestamps, since Block/Claim have no such field and both load_all bodies destructure with `..` (F3); render_ledger writes `ledger_cell(&c.id)`, which cannot alter a `C<n>` id, and the prose loop never pushes `b.id` (F4). The clause I cannot establish is the opening universal "Every input the ticket names": I was given the memo path only, not the ticket, and deliberately opened no candidate for it, so I verified the five inputs the proposition itself enumerates and not that they exhaust the ticket's list.
prose.rs: ProseEvent::Create/Revise each carry `timestamp: u64`; `cite` is the citation field; `Block` and `load_all` discard timestamps.
claims.rs: every ClaimEvent variant carries `timestamp: u64`; the loaded `Claim` has no timestamp field and `load_all` drops it — the second of the two loaders C2 says discard timestamps.
snapshot.rs: SNAPSHOT_FILES contains claims.jsonl and prose.jsonl, and snapshot_path appends `.tetel` to the memo filename — both logs ship inside `<memo>.tetel/`.

compose.rs render(): the prose loop writes heading text or paragraph text plus a `*cites:*` marker and never the block id; render_ledger writes the claim id through ledger_cell, which is identity for `C<n>`.
ledger.rs import/split_row_cells: the rendered ledger id is read back trimmed of table padding, so it is byte-identical to the workspace claim id.
SNAPSHOT_FILES ships prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl into <memo>.tetel/.
Both prose events carry timestamp: u64; cite is the citation edge; prose::load_all discards every timestamp.
Claim events carry timestamp: u64 and claims::load_all discards them too — the second loader.
render's block loop never writes b.id; render_ledger writes the claim id through ledger_cell, which is the identity for a C<n> id.

Everything C2 asserts about the tree is confirmed in source: both logs ship in `<memo>.tetel/` (snapshot.rs SNAPSHOT_FILES), every prose and claim event declares `timestamp: u64`, `cite` is the prose event's citation field, a claim id survives `ledger_cell` + `split_row_cells` byte-identical because `next_id` yields `C<n>`, both `load_all`s drop timestamps, and `compose::render` never emits a block id. What I cannot establish from source is the two clauses that attribute content to the ticket — that the ticket has the premise "the residue is computable from data tetel already holds", and that the ticket "does not name" the two consequences. The ticket lives in a repository this pass must not open, and C2 (unlike C3 and C8) does not mark that attribution as the ticket's report rather than something it establishes. Substance verified; ticket attribution unwitnessed.

records.prop: The ticket's anchor — "revised since the last grounding pass" — would have gone silent on the finding the ticket cites. `brief::build` returns every ledger claim unconditionally, including already-grounded ones ("A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on"), so every subsequent pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed and appends records with strictly later timestamps against the same digest. This is measured, not inferred: in the two shipped memos, tet28's C9 carries ten records on one unchanged digest from three passes spanning 1690 seconds, and tet28's C13 was graded `qualifies` by two passes 918 seconds apart on unchanged text. So an anchor at the *latest* grading advances past any fix-round prose edit as soon as one more pass runs — and the FORK-94 trail the ticket describes ran six rounds. The anchor must instead be the *earliest* record grading the claim's current wording: the moment that wording first entered proof, which a later pass over unchanged text cannot move.
verdicts: The mechanism and the C9 measurement hold exactly: brief::build filters nothing and its doc comment carries the quoted sentence verbatim, and tet28's C9 does have ten records on the one digest 7fa084e7 from three passes spanning 1690 s. One numeric clause is wrong: tet28's C13 pair on unchanged text (digest 65ec3111, passes 2a166dfe and c1fa7b44) is **910 seconds** apart, not 918, and no (claim, digest) group in either shipped memo's evidence log has a span of 918 s. The rest of the proposition — that a latest-grading anchor advances as soon as one more pass runs, and that the earliest in-proof record cannot be moved by a later pass — follows from the same data, but "the FORK-94 trail the ticket describes ran six rounds" rests on a ticket I was not given and did not open.
brief::build returns every ledger claim unconditionally (a bare map with no filter), and the quoted sentence appears verbatim in its doc comment.

Both numbers reproduce exactly against tet28's evidence log: C9 = ten records, one digest, three passes, 1690s span; C13 = two passes 910s apart both `qualifies` on the identical digest. The FORK-94 six-round figure is not checked here, but the proposition itself marks it as the ticket's report rather than something it re-establishes.
brief::build filters nothing and its doc comment carries the quoted sentence verbatim.

Both measured figures are exact: tet28's C9 carries 10 records on one digest from 3 passes spanning 1690s, and tet28's C13 has two `qualifies` records on the unchanged digest 65ec3111 exactly 910s apart. The clause I cannot establish is "per the ticket's own account ... the FORK-94 trail ran six rounds": the ticket lives in a planning repository this pass must not open, so even the attribution is unwitnessed here. The anchor argument itself — that only the earliest in-proof record is immovable by a later pass — is confirmed by construction (a later record with the same digest never changes min).

`brief::build` is unconditional and its doc comment carries the quoted sentence verbatim. Both numbers check out exactly: tet28 C9 has 10 records, one digest, three passes, span 1690s; tet28 C13 has two `qualifies` records on the same digest 910s apart. The only unwitnessed element is the FORK-94 six-round count, which the proposition itself explicitly records as the ticket's report rather than re-establishing, so it is not something this claim asserts on its own authority.

Clause (d) settles the ticket's two ambiguities together: the per-claim anchor is the earliest record grading the current wording, and the per-block anchor is the latest of those, so a block is listed only once its whole evidence base has settled and its text has moved since. Run against the two shipped memos it lists nothing: tet28's and tet29's post-grounding prose revisions each accompanied a claim revision, so the new wording's first proof postdates the edit, and tet28's six post-grounding revisions that did not are heading blocks. records.prop: The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its `Create` or its last `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp` on the prose event. Including creations closes an identical exposure at near-zero cost in listings. It is identical because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It is near-zero cost because a paragraph created in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not in proof when the paragraph is written; by the time any pass has put it in proof, that first proof postdates the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims.
verdicts: The mechanical half is witnessed: both `ProseEvent::Create` and `ProseEvent::Revise` carry `timestamp: u64` (F3, prose.rs:41-73), so "the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its Create or its last Revise" is implementable exactly as stated, and the rule I executed does take max(Create, latest Revise) (F6). What I cannot establish from source is the cost/benefit reasoning that the rest of the proposition asserts — that including creations is "near-zero cost in listings" because a fix-round paragraph normally cites a new claim not yet in proof. That is a claim about authoring behaviour, and the two shipped memos give no instance of it: their residue is empty under a rule that already counts creations (F6), which is consistent with the assertion but does not exhibit a single created-in-a-fix-round paragraph either being caught or being spared. The word "normally" is not measured anywhere I could reach.

Case A shows a never-revised Create is listed on its creation timestamp; cases B and C show a paragraph written before the pass that first proves its new claim is unlistable even when it also cites an already-settled claim, which is exactly the no-inflation argument. The proposition's own final sentences concede that authoring frequency is unmeasured.
ProseEvent::Create and ProseEvent::Revise both carry `timestamp: u64`, which is what makes the derivation indifferent to which kind of event bears the current text.
Both ProseEvent::Create and ProseEvent::Revise declare timestamp: u64, so the derivation is indifferent to which variant bore the current text.

A pure Create after settling is listed; a block whose cited claim is not yet in proof contributes no anchor and cannot be listed, and once that claim enters proof its first proof postdates the creation, so the block stays unlisted either way.

Both event variants carry a `timestamp` (F2), so the derivation is indifferent to Create-vs-Revise; and running the rule over tet29's real logs with synthetic creations confirms all three consequences C5 draws — a fresh paragraph under only settled claims is listed, one written before the pass that proved its new claim is not, and it is still not listed when it also cites a settled claim, because the anchor is a maximum. C5's own disclaimer about how often fix-round paragraphs take that shape is stated as unmeasured, which is accurate.

src/prose.rs is byte-identical at the pin and in the worktree. `ProseEvent` has exactly the two variants the proposition names, and both carry `timestamp: u64` — Create at line 61, Revise at line 73 — so a per-block "earliest event bearing the current text" is derivable from the log with no regard to which variant it is, exactly as stated.

What I cannot establish from source is the cost/benefit reasoning that the rest of the proposition asserts — that including creations is "near-zero cost in listings" because a fix-round paragraph normally cites a new claim not yet in proof. That is a claim about authoring behaviour, and the two shipped memos give no instance of it: their residue is empty under a rule that already counts creations (F6), which is consistent with the assertion but does not exhibit a single created-in-a-fix-round paragraph either being caught or being spared. The word "normally" is not measured anywhere I could reach.

Case A shows a never-revised Create is listed on its creation timestamp; cases B and C show a paragraph written before the pass that first proves its new claim is unlistable even when it also cites an already-settled claim, which is exactly the no-inflation argument. The proposition's own final sentences concede that authoring frequency is unmeasured.

A pure Create after settling is listed; a block whose cited claim is not yet in proof contributes no anchor and cannot be listed, and once that claim enters proof its first proof postdates the creation, so the block stays unlisted either way.

src/prose.rs is byte-identical at the pin and in the worktree. `ProseEvent` has exactly the two variants the proposition names, and both carry `timestamp: u64` — Create at line 61, Revise at line 73 — so a per-block "earliest event bearing the current text" is derivable from the log with no regard to which variant it is, exactly as stated.

records.prop: The first-proof anchor makes the line unclearable by anything that did not look at the prose, and that is deliberate: a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block. The only two things that clear it are reverting the text, and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded — which is exactly the remedy the finding calls for, since the defect is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost, stated rather than hidden: a listing has no cheap discharge, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until the memo's next claim revision, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line. This is a smaller version of a cost this project has already paid badly once — `no scope declared` printed one undischargeable line per claim and buried the findings that were about the document under a constant — but it differs where it matters: this line is about *this* document, never fires on all blocks at once, and names two concrete acts that clear it.
verdicts: The unclearable-by-re-grounding half is right: evidence is strictly appended with a fresh now_unix per record, so a later pass cannot move a claim's earliest in-proof timestamp (F7). The precedent half is right too: the `no scope declared` line did fire once per claim on every tetel-authored memo — "eight identical lines on the first real memo" — and was collapsed to one document-level line for the stated reason (F8). But the clause "The only two things that clear it are reverting the text, and revising or adding a cited claim" is false under this design's own rule. Prose history is append-only and clause (d) reads the timestamp of the event that set the block's current text; a revert is a new `Revise` with a new, later timestamp, so on tet29's real logs a block edited to 1786176064 and then reverted byte-for-byte at 1786176364 is still listed against the same anchor 1786174494 (F8). Reverting clears the line only under a different clause (d) — earliest event whose text equals the current text — which is not what C4/C5 state; C5 explicitly says the timestamp is the Create or the *last* Revise. So the enumeration of remedies has one member, not two, and the stated cost is correspondingly worse than the proposition admits.

"Under the repaired definition of a block's text timestamp ... exactly two things clear a listing" is false, and the repair is what makes the third one work. A citation-only prose revision — byte-identical text, a replacement cite list — leaves the block's text timestamp exactly where it was, because the repaired definition takes the earliest event whose text equals the current text, and changes the right-hand side of clause (d) instead. Executed against tet29's real logs: P11 rewritten at 1786174700 with no claim touched is LISTED (anchor 1786174494, cites C13); appending `C4` to its cite list — a claim already in proof since 1786175367 because a later pass genuinely regraded it — clears the listing outright. No text changed, nothing new was graded, nothing was revised for the purpose, and no machine check fires. In a fix round there is always such a claim: the one the round revised. The paragraph the residue exists to surface is laundered by pointing it at someone else's honest work. A fourth clearer follows from clause (c) rather than (d): appending a brand-new claim with no evidence at all also clears the listing, and per F2 a record-less claim is `ungrounded` — human-owed, never a machine failure — so that escape is red-free too. Note the pre-repair definition did not have this hole: a citation-only revision would have pushed the timestamp to now and the block would have stayed listed. The repair to C6 opened a second defect in C6.

The mechanism behind the refutation above, witnessed in source. `prose::revise` refuses exactly two things — an unknown block id and an empty `--why`. It does not compare the new text against the block's current text, so a revision supplying byte-identical text is accepted and appended; and `ProseEvent::Revise` carries `cite: Option<Vec<String>>`, which `load_all` applies as `b.cite = c`, a wholesale replacement. So a block's citation set is read off the LAST event that set it while its text timestamp is read off the EARLIEST event bearing the current text. C6 treats the citation set as fixed and reasons only about what can move the timestamp; it is the other side of clause (d) that is freely mutable at zero cost. This is also the documented remedial path: prose.rs's own doc on the `cite` parameter says it exists so that `tetel review`'s instruction "mint the missing claim and cite it" is reachable for existing prose.

Everything about unclearability holds as executed: re-grounding on unchanged wording leaves P11 listed (the anchor is a minimum, and a later duplicate record cannot move it), a citation-only revision to an in-proof claim lists rather than clears, a record-less citation contributes no anchor, and only a byte-exact revert or moving the evidence clears. The clause that fails as written is "never fires on all blocks at once". tet29's shipped prose is 12 blocks, all non-heading and all cited; appending one post-proof flow-edit revision to each lists all 12 of 12. The rule does not structurally exclude a whole-document listing — what distinguishes it from `no scope declared` is that it is conditional on what the author did, not that a full sweep is impossible.

records.prop: This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. Both sides are produced by a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the two places it is defined — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, the only two definitions in the worktree — so they are the same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock; `SystemTime::now()` reads the clock of whoever called it. The bound is therefore exact and must be printed rather than implied: an ordering this line reports can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large.
verdicts: The substance holds: there are exactly two `fn now_unix` definitions in the worktree, at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, both `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)`, so the two sides are the same unit and epoch (UTC seconds, no timezone term), and nothing establishes the two processes shared a wall clock — `SystemTime::now()` reads the caller's clock. Two clauses are wrong as written. (a) "byte-identical in the two places it is defined": the bytes differ — workspace.rs:257 is `pub fn` with the chain on one line, evidence.rs:288 is a private `fn` with the same chain split across four indented lines. The expressions are token-identical, not byte-identical. (b) "This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes": `facts::mint_windows` already compares a `FactEvent::Create` timestamp from facts.jsonl against refusals.log timestamps (`ts <= *minted_at`), and each mint and each refusal is a separate process invocation. What is genuinely new is comparing an *authoring-side* clock against a *grounding-side* clock, which is not what the sentence says.

Both stated line numbers are exact (workspace.rs:257 pub fn, one-line body; evidence.rs:288 private fn, four-line body), the chains are token-for-token identical, mint_windows is the named precedent and is workspace-local, and EvidenceRecord::timestamp is explicitly read by no check. `SystemTime::now()` reading the caller's clock and the unbounded-from-below interval are both stated as limits rather than claims, which is what the code supports.

analyze_ledger is the check that compares a claim against its evidence, and it does so by sha256 digest, never by timestamp — C7's "every check that could have compared a claim against its evidence has used a digest instead".

workspace.rs:257 is the one-line `pub fn now_unix`; evidence.rs:288 is the private four-line one; the SystemTime chain is token-for-token identical, so same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, no timezone term, and each reads its own caller's clock.
facts::mint_windows does compare a mint timestamp against refusals.log timestamps written by separate invocations, and both logs belong to one workspace.

A whole-source search for `timestamp` finds no other comparison site: no existing check orders an authoring timestamp against a grounding-pass one, and the evidence record's timestamp is read by nothing.

`mint_windows` does order timestamps written by separate invocations (fact mints against refusals.log lines) and does it inside one workspace; and a survey of checks.rs, scope.rs, worldstate.rs, evidence.rs, review.rs and citations.rs finds no timestamp comparison at all, with the identity `born` field never read by a check — so no existing check compares an authoring clock against a grounding pass's, and claim-versus-evidence is done by digest in `analyze_ledger`.

The line references are exact: workspace.rs:257 is the `pub fn` with its body on one line, evidence.rs:288 is a private fn whose identical chain runs over four lines, and the expression is token-for-token the same — UTC seconds since the Unix epoch with no timezone term. The prose side is stamped by the first and the evidence side by the second, and both call `SystemTime::now()`, which reads the calling process's own clock and records nothing about which clock that was. So "sound in unit but not in clock" is exactly right, and the stated bound follows.

records.prop: This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. Both sides are produced by a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the two places it is defined — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, the only two definitions in the worktree — so they are the same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock; `SystemTime::now()` reads the clock of whoever called it. The bound is therefore exact and must be printed rather than implied: an ordering this line reports can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large.

records.prop: The vacuous cases are excluded by the in-proof gate rather than by a special case, and the exclusion is justified by non-overlap: a claim with no records at all is already printed as `ungrounded`, and a claim whose every record grades superseded text is already a machine failure as `out_of_proof`, so a prose block resting on either is already in front of the reader under a line that says something truer about it. Requiring every cited claim to be in proof therefore makes a memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo mid-first-draft, list nothing at all — the residue is empty until a memo has been graded, which is when it starts being able to say anything. Two populations fall outside the rule and are worth naming rather than counting: heading blocks, and paragraphs that cite nothing. A paragraph with no citation is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare against, so its invisibility here is a real gap and belongs in the printed non-coverage list, not in a footnote.
verdicts: Second record for the non-overlap clause: `ungrounded_claims` prints "ungrounded — no evidence record on file" in the human-owed partition and `out_of_proof` is one of the eleven fields in `machine_check_failed`, so a claim with no records and a claim whose every record is stale are each already in front of the reader under their own line.

The non-overlap justification holds only for a block ALL of whose citations are ungrounded or out of proof, but the gate C9 defends is universally quantified ("Requiring every cited claim to be in proof"). For a block citing nine settled claims and one record-less one, the substitute line the reader gets is `ungrounded: C99` — a statement about a claim, not about the paragraph, and in no sense "truer about it" than the residue line it displaced, which would have said this paragraph's text postdates every settled claim it rests on. Escape B above shows this is not merely a gap but an actuator: appending one record-less claim to a listed block's cite list removes it from the residue while adding only a human-owed `ungrounded` line and no machine failure. The exclusion needs the condition stated, or the gate needs to be per-citation rather than all-or-nothing.
Both vacuous cases list nothing with no special rule — the in-proof test alone produces the behaviour.
Heading blocks (case D) and paragraphs citing nothing (case E) fall outside the rule entirely, the two populations C9 names as non-covered.

records.prop: The residue is bullets in the existing flat human-owed list, not a new section, and it is identified by document line as well as by block id. The partition has no sub-headings — it is one list of `  - ` entries, some of which already run to several indented lines, as `mint_windows` and `tree_states` do — so a section would be the only one there and would say by its shape that it outranks the rest. One entry per listed block, plus a single preamble entry carrying what is constant across them: that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same. Printing that constant once rather than in every bullet follows the precedent this crate set when `no scope declared` was collapsed to one document-level line, on the stated grounds that repeating a constant per row "buried the findings that are about *this* document under a constant". The entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because `compose::render` never writes a block's id into the output and an id alone names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find; the offsets come from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render` so that the block-to-line mapping is described in exactly one place. It also names each cited claim, that claim's first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, so a reader can disbelieve the conclusion.
verdicts: Every checkable clause holds: the human-owed partition is one flat list of `  - ` entries with no sub-heading anywhere in it; the mint_windows and tree_states entries already run to further six-space-indented lines; and the `no scope declared` constant is printed once at document level under the comment ending "buried the findings that are about *this* document under a constant", quoted byte-for-byte in the proposition. The reason the entry must name a document line — that `compose::render` never writes a block's id into the output — is separately witnessed (F4).

Second record: the prose loop in compose::render pushes only text, heading markers and the `*cites:*` line — never `b.id` — so a listing identified by block id alone would name something a reader holding only the memo cannot locate, which is the proposition's stated reason for adding a document line.

Anchor points verified: check_file already loads the evidence records (`let (evidence_records, evidence_errors) = evidence::load(path)?`) and its `if snapshot_dir.is_dir()` block is exactly where notes_outside_extent, tree_states, uncensused_targets, unquoted_premises and mint_windows are computed, so a call added there is beside the named neighbours and is silently skipped without a snapshot.

Second record: `Findings` and `machine_check_failed` are in checks.rs and the eleven-field OR does not include any human-owed field, so a new field left out of it is human-owed by construction; `NON_COVERAGE` is the `&[&str]` in report.rs printed as a trailing `  - tetel does not catch:` loop, so new entries have a home; and the existing missing-snapshot bullet ("no workspace snapshot beside this document...") is already printed. prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl already ship in SNAPSHOT_FILES (F2), so nothing new ships.

The implementation surface holds only under a condition it does not state: that every claim's proposition survives the ledger round trip byte-exact. C11 tells the implementer to compute the list "from the snapshot's `prose.jsonl` and `claims.jsonl` plus the evidence records `check_file` has already loaded", but `check_file` does not digest claims.jsonl — it builds `ledger::import(&doc.body)` from the rendered document and hands those claims to `analyze_ledger`, and `brief_file` briefs a grounding pass from the same source, so every `proposition_digest` in the evidence log is over the document-derived text. Between the two, `compose::ledger_cell` replaces every `\n` with a space and `ledger::split_row_cells` trims each cell. Pipes round-trip; newlines and edge whitespace do not. grep does not implement the ticket's first constraint — "an explicitly named path must still be read; only traversal skips" — and delegating that constraint to grep's flags would silently break it. Measured on BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD: a file named explicitly on the command line is skipped when `--exclude` matches it (no output, exit 1, against output and exit 0 for the identical command without the flag), and a directory named explicitly as the recursion root is skipped when `--exclude-dir` matches it (same contrast). Only one of the three cases behaves the way the constraint describes: `--exclude-dir` does not suppress a file inside an excluded directory when that file is named explicitly and searched non-recursively.

The rendered-memo exclusion the ticket sketches — "one glob for `*.tetel` directories under the search root, with the suffix stripped, passed as `--exclude`" — is unsound as written, in two independent ways measured on BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD. First, a pattern must be spelled the way grep constructs the file's name from the root as given: with a relative root, an absolute-path `--exclude` excluded nothing at all and the search returned every file, while the same path spelled relative to the root excluded exactly the intended file. Second, a suffix-stripped bare basename over-excludes: `--exclude='memo.md'` removed both a genuine rendered memo and an unrelated other/memo.md that has no sibling other/memo.md.tetel and so is not a rendered memo under the ticket's own test. The exclusion must therefore be emitted path-prefixed in the root's own spelling, never as a basename.

records.prop: The exclusion disclosure can be made durable with no schema change, by writing it into the whole-search record's `label`. Two existing mechanisms carry it from there: `compose::render_facts` builds the committed memo's "Extent (captured)" column by joining extent entries' `label` fields and renders nothing else from an entry — not the `key`, not the captured output — so a label reaches every reader of the committed document; and `facts::mint` hashes each pending entry's `label` (followed by `world_root`, `world_state` and `output`) into the pin, so two searches whose exclusion sets differ pin differently even when their matched output is byte-identical.

The ticket's central measurement reproduces on this tree, and the three exclusions together remove tetel's own output from a census without removing source. A census of the symbol NON_COVERAGE over the tetel worktree with `look_grep`'s flags returned 87 lines / 858,096 bytes from 15 files, of which 14 were tetel's own output — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot .jsonl files — and exactly one, src/report.rs, was source. With `--exclude-dir='*.tetel'`, `--exclude='*.evidence.jsonl'` and one path-spelled `--exclude` per stripped snapshot directory, the same census returned 2 lines / 169 bytes, from src/report.rs alone.

Set those aside and the file set is exactly the 15 claimed, with exactly the claimed composition — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot .jsonl, and src/report.rs as the sole source. The post-exclusion figure is exact: 2 lines / 169 bytes, src/report.rs alone. So the clause I cannot establish is the specific "87 lines / 858,096 bytes"; the substance and every other figure hold.

records.prop: A change confined to `look_grep` cannot alter how an already-committed memo checks, for two independent reasons. The first is call-graph isolation: two exhaustive greps of the whole `src/` tree show `Command::new` matching in only `observe.rs` (the grep inside `look_grep`, and `run_command`'s child) and `worldstate.rs` (git), and `observe::` matching in only `main.rs` and `mcp.rs`, which build a `LookRequest` and dispatch it, and `facts.rs`, where the sole occurrence is inside a doc comment — so every other file in `src/`, including every file on the check and render paths, neither calls into `observe` by that path nor spawns a process by that constructor. The second is immutability: the `tetel fact` module doc states that a revision rewrites the note only, and that "extent, output and pin are set once at mint time and never appear in a revision event at all, so there is no code path that could change them later either". A fact minted under the old behaviour therefore keeps the extent and pin it was minted with, whatever a later `look` would now do.

Capping what a fact stores and capping what a `look` returns are already separable in practice, and only the return path currently has any cap at all — imposed downstream, not by tetel. Taking this design's one census, `look --grep look_grep` rooted at the tetel worktree, the search succeeded and was recorded, but the agent harness refused to return the result, reporting 707,751 characters across 38 lines as exceeding its maximum allowed tokens and spilling it to a file; the author therefore never read the output of their own census, while the full captured output was nonetheless minted into the fact and ships in the snapshot. The census's own extent shows why: of the ten files matched, eight are tetel's own output — three snapshot `facts.jsonl`, one snapshot `claims.jsonl`, one snapshot `prose.jsonl`, two evidence ledgers and one rendered memo — and two, `src/observe.rs` and `src/worldstate.rs`, are source.
verdicts: Reproduced independently: the same census on the same client was refused by the harness with a character count and a spill file, while the search was recorded in full; the design's 707,751 characters / 38 lines / 10 files, and the exact composition (eight tetel artifacts, src/observe.rs and src/worldstate.rs), reconstruct byte-exactly once this memo's own artifacts are filtered out. The only clause I could not witness is that the *author* never read their own output, which is a fact about their session.

Source side of the separability claim: look_grep's return is `printed.push_str(&stdout)` with no cap, and the per-file pending entries carry `output: matches.join("\n")` with no cap either — so tetel imposes no bound on either path, and any bound that fires is the caller's.

The extent breakdown is exact and the size/harness clauses are not checkable here. Re-running the census `look_grep`-pattern search over the tetel worktree today and setting aside the six tet46 artifacts that did not exist at measurement time yields precisely the ten files claimed, in precisely the claimed composition: three snapshot facts.jsonl, one snapshot claims.jsonl, one snapshot prose.jsonl, two evidence ledgers, one rendered memo, and src/observe.rs plus src/worldstate.rs as the two source files. What I cannot establish is the clause "reporting 707,751 characters across 38 lines as exceeding its maximum allowed tokens and spilling it to a file" — that is an event in the author's own client session, not something recoverable from this repository, and the same search now returns 110 lines / 2,498,237 bytes. I deliberately did not reproduce it by taking a multi-hundred-kilobyte `look` myself, since minting that would put the whole output permanently into a snapshot.
The source half: look_grep copies the whole grep stdout into LookOutcome with no cap of any kind, so no cap on what a fact stores or on what a look returns exists inside tetel.

verdicts: Reproduced independently: the same census on the same client was refused by the harness with a character count and a spill file, while the search was recorded in full; the design's 707,751 characters / 38 lines / 10 files, and the exact composition (eight tetel artifacts, src/observe.rs and src/worldstate.rs), reconstruct byte-exactly once this memo's own artifacts are filtered out. The only clause I could not witness is that the *author* never read their own output, which is a fact about their session.

Source side of the separability claim: look_grep's return is `printed.push_str(&stdout)` with no cap, and the per-file pending entries carry `output: matches.join("\n")` with no cap either — so tetel imposes no bound on either path, and any bound that fires is the caller's.

The extent breakdown is exact and the size/harness clauses are not checkable here. Re-running the census `look_grep`-pattern search over the tetel worktree today and setting aside the six tet46 artifacts that did not exist at measurement time yields precisely the ten files claimed, in precisely the claimed composition: three snapshot facts.jsonl, one snapshot claims.jsonl, one snapshot prose.jsonl, two evidence ledgers, one rendered memo, and src/observe.rs plus src/worldstate.rs as the two source files. What I cannot establish is the clause "reporting 707,751 characters across 38 lines as exceeding its maximum allowed tokens and spilling it to a file" — that is an event in the author's own client session, not something recoverable from this repository, and the same search now returns 110 lines / 2,498,237 bytes. I deliberately did not reproduce it by taking a multi-hundred-kilobyte `look` myself, since minting that would put the whole output permanently into a snapshot.
The source half: look_grep copies the whole grep stdout into LookOutcome with no cap of any kind, so no cap on what a fact stores or on what a look returns exists inside tetel.

records.prop: `check`'s standing non-coverage list needs a second line rather than an amendment to the one it has. The existing entry reads "whatever the platform's grep skipped — symlinked directories and binary files bound what a whole-worktree search physically visited": both causes it names are platform accidents, and nothing in it contemplates something tetel itself declined to visit. Every entry is a static string and none is per-search, so the standing line can only say that the policy exists; what a given search actually excluded is not something this list can carry.

TET-28's census predicate needs no change, and this is what makes the two disclosures divide cleanly. `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads exactly five things — that the kind is `Search` or `NoMatch`, that the pattern byte-equals the symbol, that `world_root` is non-empty and not `NO_GIT`, and that `key == world_root` — and never reads `label` or `output`. A worktree-rooted search therefore still censuses after this change, correctly, because the predicate was always about a search's existence and rooting rather than about what it found. What changes is not the predicate but what a passing census entitles a reader to conclude, and that is carried by text: a standing line in `check` saying the exclusion policy exists, and the search record's own `label` saying which patterns this particular search was given.

records.prop: "No `look` returns tetel's own content" is not the honest name for what this design builds, and the honest name is better rather than merely narrower: a `look` returns tetel's own output only when the caller named it. `look_path` refuses a directory and reads exactly the one file it was given, with no traversal of any kind, so every file it can ever return is one the caller named explicitly and it is left unchanged by this design. `look_grep` is where the whole mechanism lands, and its rule is the same sentence applied to a search — the exclusions are passed only when the root is a directory that is not itself tetel content, so what they remove is only ever reached by traversal. Stating the guarantee over naming rather than over `look`'s two modes covers both with one sentence and does not promise a reader something `look_path` never did.
verdicts: look_path's half is exact: directory refusal, single fs::read_to_string, no traversal, therefore every file it can return was named by the caller and no exclusion applies to it.

look_grep's half: `-r` is added only when the root is a directory, so traversal — the only way a file the caller did not name can be reached — happens exactly in the case where the design says exclusions are passed.

records.prop: No opt-out flag should be added, because three escape hatches already exist and each is reached by naming something rather than by setting a flag. `look_path` opens any single named file, including one inside a snapshot, and is untouched by this design. `look --grep` rooted at a path that is itself tetel content passes no exclusions at all, which is not merely permitted but forced: grep's `--exclude-dir` suppresses a directory named as the recursion root, so the flags must be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would return nothing. And `run` spawns `argv` directly with nothing between the empty-argv refusal and the spawn that inspects, parses or classifies the command or the paths it will touch, so it has no place a path exclusion could be applied even in principle. A flag would add a fourth route that, unlike all three of these, leaves no trace in what was named.
verdicts: Escape hatches 1 and 3: look_path opens any single named file with no traversal and nothing in this design touches it; run_command has only the empty-argv refusal between entry and `Command::new(&argv[0]).spawn()`, with no inspection of the command or its paths, so it offers no place to apply an exclusion.

Escape hatch 2 and its "not merely permitted but forced": measured, `--exclude-dir='*.tetel'` applied to a recursion root that is itself a *.tetel directory returns nothing and exits 1, so the flags must be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would yield no output.

records.prop: The pin's non-stationarity is relocated rather than removed, and the relocation is the improvement. Measured on a scratch tree: rendering a second memo into it, changing no source, left the matched output of a search for the same symbol byte-identical while changing the emitted exclusion list from one rendered-memo pattern to two. So the captured output is now stationary against tetel's own churn — which was the ticket's within-run complaint, since an evidence ledger growing during grading no longer reaches the search at all — but the exclusion set is not, and because the design writes that set into the search record's label and the label is inside the pin, two censuses of the same symbol against the same source will still pin differently across a render. The difference is that the cause is now written in plain text in the same record, instead of being an invisible change in what the search happened to read.
verdicts: The "label is inside the pin" step: facts::mint hashes each pending entry's label first in the pin input, so an exclusion set written into the search record's label makes two otherwise identical censuses pin differently.
The pin half: facts::mint hashes each pending entry's label into the pin, so an exclusion set written into the search record's label changes the pin even when the matched output is byte-identical.

records.prop: A directory containing nothing but tetel's output is still not "explicitly named", and the cost of that is concrete rather than theoretical. `docs/design` holds exactly nine entries — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, three snapshot directories — and nothing else. A search rooted there for the symbol `census` returns 184 lines and 1,200,881 bytes today; under this rule it returns nothing and exits 1. The alternative, treating a directory as named when everything beneath it happens to be tetel's, is a judgement about a directory's contents rather than a test on a path, and the project rules that out as a refusal trigger. So the exclusion stays a format test on the root itself, and the price is that searching across memos requires naming a memo file or a snapshot directory rather than the folder they sit in.
verdicts: The "project rules that out" clause is backed by README.md's stated rule that refusals are format-level and never heuristic; a contents-based judgement about a directory is not a decidable format test.

Two clauses do not hold as written today. "docs/design holds exactly nine entries" — it holds twelve, in four triples of the described shape; the extra triple is tet46's own memo/ledger/snapshot, untracked, so the nine was correct before this memo was rendered. And "returns 184 lines and 1,200,881 bytes today" — the same search now returns 260 lines and 2,996,478 bytes. The load-bearing half is exact: with the root docs/design (a directory with no `.tetel` component, so exclusions are passed), the three exclusions leave nothing at all — no output, exit 1, as measured. I did not attempt to verify the separate assertion that "the project rules that out as a refusal trigger", which is a statement about project rules rather than about this repository's source.

records.prop: The invariance of the three committed memos was demonstrated rather than only argued, against the one input the proposed mechanism actually depends on. `tetel check` was run over tet28's, tet29's and tet30's memos while docs/design held three snapshot directories, and again after this memo was rendered there, making four — a change in exactly the set of tetel artifacts from which the exclusion set would be computed. All three memos produced byte-identical output across the two runs: the same exit code, the same byte count, and the same SHA-256 of combined stdout and stderr (3cdf677b… / 5097feb5… / b3bca4fd…).
verdicts: I could not verify the demonstration and could not reproduce its numbers. All three memos do check clean (exit 0) with output that is byte-stable across repeated runs, but at the post-render state the SHA-256 of combined stdout+stderr is 1955453e… / c6cff384… / ade4a129… (14974 / 13095 / 68142 bytes) — none of which begins 3cdf677b, 5097feb5 or b3bca4fd. That mismatch is explainable without contradicting the claim (check's output embeds a "checked by tetel 0.1.0 build …" line, and any difference in binary or capture recipe changes the hash), but it means I am not confirming the quoted values. More fundamentally, the pre-render state — docs/design holding three snapshot directories — no longer exists, so the before/after comparison the claim reports cannot be re-run here at all; the clause "All three memos produced byte-identical output across the two runs" is the one I could not establish.

kept.clause: The invariance of the three committed memos was demonstrated rather than only argued, against the one input the proposed mechanism actually depends on.
kept.why: The captured commands and directory listings do not establish that the proposed mechanism depends on exactly one input.

records.prop: Owed rules 1 and 2 can be taken directly from `analyze_ledger`'s existing outputs — rule 1 is membership in `ungrounded_claims` (no evidence record at all for the claim id) and rule 2 is membership in `out_of_proof` (records exist, all with a digest differing from `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`) — with no new predicate over records needed for either.
verdicts: Rule 1 is exact: `ungrounded` is pushed under `if records.is_empty()`, i.e. no evidence record at all for the claim id, and needs no new predicate. Rule 2's parenthetical gloss is not: out_of_proof is populated only when at least one record has a NON-EMPTY digest differing from current AND no record has a digest equal to current. Both `fresh` and `stale` are computed after `.filter(|r| !r.proposition_digest.is_empty())`, so a claim whose records all carry empty (pre-digest) digests yields no stale record and is therefore NOT in out_of_proof — even though "all with a digest differing from sha256_hex(claim.proposition)" is literally true of it. Second, smaller: out_of_proof is a `Vec<String>` of multi-line rendered messages (one per stale record, id-prefixed), not a set of claim ids, so "membership in out_of_proof" is not a set test as written. The substantive assertion — both rules come out of analyze_ledger's existing outputs with no new predicate over records — holds.

Everything up to the last sentence checks out exactly: rule 1 is `records.is_empty()` on the unfiltered per-id record set; rule 2's condition is precisely "at least one non-empty-digest record and none equal to sha256_hex(proposition)", since out_of_proof is pushed only inside the `stale` loop under `fresh.is_empty()`; and a claim whose records all carry empty digests falls out of the fresh/stale partition (both are taken after `.filter(|r| !r.proposition_digest.is_empty())`) while still having records, so it is in neither set. The failing clause is "Both outputs are rendered message strings rather than id sets, so consuming them for scheduling means `analyze_ledger` reporting the ids alongside the messages." That is true of `out_of_proof` (`Vec<String>`, id only interpolated into a formatted message) but false of `ungrounded_claims`, which is declared `Vec<(String, String)>` and documented as `(id, proposition)` — the id is already a separate field, so no new reporting is needed for rule 1.

Every operative part checks out in src/checks.rs:638-860: `ungrounded` is pushed as `(claim.id.clone(), claim.proposition.clone())` into a `Vec<(String,String)>`; `out_of_proof` is pushed only inside `for r in &stale` when `fresh.is_empty()`, i.e. exactly when the claim has at least one record with a non-empty digest and none whose digest equals `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`; and out_of_proof entries are rendered multi-line message strings carrying no separate id field, while ungrounded already carries ids. The clause I cannot let stand as written is the causal one: "A claim whose records all carry empty pre-digest digests is in neither set, because both partitions are taken after those records are filtered out." The conclusion is true, but the stated reason only explains the out_of_proof half. Exclusion from `ungrounded_claims` does not follow from the filter at all — the guard is `if records.is_empty()` over the UNFILTERED record list (checks.rs:721), so such a claim escapes `ungrounded` because it has records, not because anything was filtered out of a partition.

Every clause checks out: `ungrounded` is pushed as `(claim.id.clone(), claim.proposition.clone())` and the return type's first element is `Vec<(String, String)>`; `out_of_proof` is pushed per stale record only when `fresh.is_empty()`, where the stale/fresh partition is taken over `records.iter().filter(|r| !r.proposition_digest.is_empty())`, so it fires exactly for a claim with at least one non-empty-digest record and none equal to `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`; an all-empty-digest claim is filtered out of that partition entirely and also escapes `ungrounded`, whose test is `records.is_empty()` over the unfiltered list; and `out_of_proof` is a `Vec<String>` of rendered multi-line messages, with the id embedded in the text rather than carried as a field, while `ungrounded` already carries ids.

Every mechanical statement in this claim checks out against checks.rs 630-800: `ungrounded` on `records.is_empty()`, `out_of_proof` on a stale record with `fresh.is_empty()`, the empty-digest claim escaping both, and `out_of_proof` being rendered strings rather than ids. The qualification is on the instruction the claim ends with — "only it needs the claim ids reported alongside the messages" — which tells an implementer to widen `analyze_ledger`'s return type. That widening buys nothing. Both sets entail zero `fresh` records by the guards that populate them, and the floor disjunct counts a subset of `fresh`, so every claim in `ungrounded` or `out_of_proof` is already owed under the floor for any N >= 1. Rules 1 and 2 add no member to the owed set, so the ids they would supply are never the reason a claim appears in it. The claim is true about what the code does and about what reusing these sets would require; it does not establish that reusing them is required.

Each clause checks against the source: ungrounded is pushed under `records.is_empty()` over the unfiltered per-id list; out_of_proof is pushed only inside `for r in &stale` under `if fresh.is_empty()`. Both therefore imply zero records with digest == current (an empty digest can never equal a non-empty sha256 hex). The empty-digest-only case is correctly described: those records are filtered out before the partition, so stale is empty and the loop never runs, while records is non-empty so ungrounded is skipped — and such a claim still has no exact digest match.

Both guards read as stated (records.is_empty(); fresh.is_empty() inside the stale loop), and the residual empty-digest case is exactly as described: non-empty records, empty stale, zero exact digest matches.

records.prop: Every evidence record already stores a pin — on the witnessed path the pin of the grounder's own fact, i.e. the tree it stood in, written expressly so that "was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?" becomes measurable — in a field no check reads today; so rule 3 is implementable as a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written, whereas folding the pin into `sha256_hex` would change every pinned claim's current digest and drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof`.
verdicts: Rule 3 is not implementable as the comparison this claim decides on. Ran the worktree's own binary as `brief --json` over every memo in docs/design: 87 claims across five ledgers (tet28/29/30/46/47), and ZERO carry a `pin` — `render_json` emits the field only when `Claim::pin` is `Some`, so `find_stated_pin` returns None for every document in this corpus, TET-47's own included. Meanwhile every witnessed record in tet30's ledger carries `Some("sha256:...")`. The comparison therefore has no second operand anywhere it would run: either None short-circuits and rule 3 is dead code that never fires on any existing memo, or Some != None and every claim of every existing memo is permanently owed under rule 3 alone — which discharges the entire cost saving the design is for. The claim's own qualifier "answerable on ledgers already written" is the part that fails: the ledgers are written, the memos have no stated pin to answer against. The design states neither behaviour for the None case.

Second, independent refutation of the same clause: the two values compared are not the same kind of thing. src/facts.rs lines 405-452 constructs a fact's pin as `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending entry's label, world_root, world_state and output — a content fingerprint of the observation, with no relation to any commit id. src/ledger.rs lines 150-205 takes the claim's pin as the last backticked token after the word "pin" in the prose window before the ledger table, under the documented corpus convention "at pin `71c0fd1`" — a git short hash typed by an author. So even on a memo that did state a pin, the comparison is `sha256:<64 hex>` against `71c0fd1`, which is unequal by construction. The claim's premise — that the stored pin is "the tree it stood in" — treats a content hash of one fact's captured bytes as a tree identifier; two facts taken in the same checkout at the same commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ, which is nearly always.

The load-bearing identification is wrong on two counts. (1) A witnessed record's `pin` is `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending extent entry's label + world_root + world_state + output (src/facts.rs:414-436) — a content fingerprint of the observation, not "the tree it stood in". The tree it stood in is carried by a different field, `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, and it is that field, not `pin`, that carries the doc comment the proposition quotes ("Nothing reads it yet. It is written now so the question it exists for — *was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?* — becomes measurable at all"). (2) A claim's currently stated pin is the backticked token parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` — a short git hash such as `abc1234`/`deadbee` in the crate's own tests. A `sha256:`-prefixed observation fingerprint can never equal one, so "a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written" would fire on every witnessed-grounded claim unconditionally rather than detecting a re-pin. The comparison the design wants is against `world`. Two subsidiary clauses do hold: no check reads the record pin today (F5), and folding the pin into `sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` would indeed drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof` (F3). "Every evidence record already stores a pin" is also too strong on the ingested path, where `RecordInput.pin` is `#[serde(default)] Option<String>` and a record written without one stores `None`.

Everything structural holds — a fact's pin is `sha256:` over each observation entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (a content fingerprint, not a tree identifier); a claim's pin is a backticked prose token; every witnessed record's predicate carries the deduped world markers of the fact's extent; `check` reads the authoring tree states out of the shipped facts.jsonl; and `world` is present on `Predicate` but absent from `EvidenceRecord`, so it is dropped at read-back in `parse_line`. The clause that fails is the count. Replaying `brief --json` over the five rendered memos at this commit gives 15 + 14 + 13 + 19 + 27 = 88 claims, not 87, with zero `pin` keys among them. The "missing from all" property is exact; the population is 88.

The count does not. Replaying `brief --json` over the five rendered memos at this commit gives 15 + 14 + 13 + 19 + 27 = 88 claims with zero `pin` keys, not 87. "Missing from all" is exact; the population is 88.

On the absent second operand I confirmed the four memos other than the one under grading carry no `pin` in `brief --json` (0 of 61 items), and the grounding brief for the fifth prints no `pin:` line for any of its 32 claims, so the corpus figure holds for all five.

Both halves check out as written. The fact pin is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each entry's label, world_root, world_state and output — a content fingerprint. And `brief --json` over all five rendered memos yields 89 claims with zero `pin` keys, so the claim-side operand is universally absent; the disjunction the proposition draws from that (never fires, or every claim permanently owed) follows.

The measured half is right and the conclusion survives, but the universal the claim reaches for is false. "The comparison has no second operand anywhere it would run" is asserted from a survey of the five tetel-RENDERED memos. It does not hold on the other population the tool serves: `brief --json` over tests/fixtures/ledger_check.md, an imported hand-authored ledger, returns both claims carrying "pin": "abc1234", and tests/brief_cli.rs:53 asserts that the document-level pin is attached to each claim. On an imported ledger the operand is present, so the rule would run rather than short-circuit, and the two-case split the claim closes on ("either the absent value short-circuits and the rule never fires, or it reads as a mismatch and every claim of every existing memo is permanently owed") is missing that case. Rule 3 should still be dropped — a git short-hash lifted from prose and a sha256 content fingerprint over an observation's labels and output are different kinds of value and would mismatch wherever the comparison did run — but the ground is kind-mismatch, not universal absence, and this matters more now that the other stated ground for dropping rule 3 (C29's "unsatisfiable forever after") does not hold.

Holds only for WITNESSED records, a restriction the proposition does not state. C6 asserts flatly that "a record's pin is a fact's `sha256:` fingerprint" and that the two pins "can never be equal, so on the imported population the comparison fires on every claim always". `record` has two write paths and only the witnessed one sets `pin: Some(fact.pin.clone())`. On the ingested path `build_statement` sets `pin: input.pin.clone()` from `RecordInput.pin`, caller-supplied free text copied verbatim with no shape check (F1). The imported population is precisely where claim pins exist — the crate's own fixture pins both claims `abc1234` — so a reporter filing an ingested record there may type `abc1234` and the two pins are equal. On that population the comparison therefore does not fire always; it is dischargeable by naming, which is the same defect C24 names for `pass` and which it fixes by counting witnessed records only. Rule 3's section never applies that restriction. The decision to drop rule 3 survives, but the reason as written is wrong for half the population it invokes: the correct statement is that the comparison is either vacuous (tetel-rendered, no claim pin) or discharge-by-typing (imported, ingested records), not that it always fires.

The two forms can never be byte-equal, so a kind-mismatch comparison fires on every pinned claim always.
Second population confirmed: across the four other rendered memos' 61 briefed claims not one item carries a `pin` key, so on the tetel-rendered population the comparison fires on none.

Witnessed pin is Some(fact.pin), and a fact's pin is "sha256:" + sha256 over each extent entry's label, world_root, world_state and output; ledger_check.md's two claims both take the prose pin abc1234; build_statement copies input.pin verbatim with no validation.

(1) A witnessed record's `pin` is `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` over each pending extent entry's label + world_root + world_state + output (src/facts.rs:414-436) — a content fingerprint of the observation, not "the tree it stood in". The tree it stood in is carried by a different field, `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, and it is that field, not `pin`, that carries the doc comment the proposition quotes ("Nothing reads it yet. It is written now so the question it exists for — *was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?* — becomes measurable at all"). (2) A claim's currently stated pin is the backticked token parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` — a short git hash such as `abc1234`/`deadbee` in the crate's own tests. A `sha256:`-prefixed observation fingerprint can never equal one, so "a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written" would fire on every witnessed-grounded claim unconditionally rather than detecting a re-pin. The comparison the design wants is against `world`. Two subsidiary clauses do hold: no check reads the record pin today (F5), and folding the pin into `sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` would indeed drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof` (F3). Everything structural holds — a fact's pin is `sha256:` over each observation entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (a content fingerprint, not a tree identifier); a claim's pin is a backticked prose token; every witnessed record's predicate carries the deduped world markers of the fact's extent; `check` reads the authoring tree states out of the shipped facts.jsonl; and `world` is present on `Predicate` but absent from `EvidenceRecord`, so it is dropped at read-back in `parse_line`. The "missing from all" property is exact; the population is 88.

Holds only for WITNESSED records, a restriction the proposition does not state. records.prop: Because one parsed pin is assigned to every claim under a ledger table, a pin change is a document-level event: rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it, so it is a re-pin detector for the memo rather than a per-claim scheduling condition.
verdicts: The premise is exactly right — `import` parses one `Option<String>` per ledger table and clones it into every `Claim` under that table, so the *stated* pin side of the comparison is uniform across the table. The conclusion drawn from it, "rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it", does not follow, because rule 3 compares the stated pin against a value stored per *record*, and records accumulate per claim. Immediately after a re-pin the disjunction holds; once any subset of claims has been re-graded against the new pin, their records carry it and the rule fires on the remainder only — i.e. it becomes precisely the per-claim scheduling condition the proposition says it is not. The weaker reading ("a pin change is a document-level event") is supported; the strict all-or-none clause is not.

The inference is invalid as given; the conclusion survives only degenerately. "One parsed pin is assigned to every claim" establishes uniformity on ONE side of rule 3's comparison. Whether the comparison's result is uniform across the table depends on the other side too, and that side is not uniform: tet30's single ledger holds 61 distinct record pin values, and every one of its 13 claims carries records with several different pins (C11: 16 distinct). A record's pin is the grounder's own fact fingerprint (src/facts.rs 405-452), minted per observation, so it varies per record, per claim and per pass. "Rule 3 fires for every claim in the table or for none of it" is therefore true today only because the two operands are drawn from disjoint namespaces and never match at all — a vacuous uniformity, not the document-level re-pin detector the claim describes. Make the comparison meaningful in any way, and a claim last graded by a pass standing at the memo's pin and a claim last graded by a pass standing elsewhere get different answers within the same table, which is exactly the per-claim behaviour this claim rules out.

records.prop: Rule 5's matching rule should be the crate's existing `citation_ids_in` rather than a new `C\d+` scan: the existing matcher is already the definition of a row→row citation edge for the dependency-cascade check, it is id-shape-agnostic (a `C\d+` regex would miss real ids of the `R-ROOT` / `CYC-A` shape the crate's own fixtures use, a genuine false-negative class), and its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading.
verdicts: "Its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading" holds only under a condition the claim does not state: that every inter-claim reference an author writes inside a proposition is bracketed or sits in a whole-line cites trailer. It is not. `scan_line` (src/citations.rs 55-140) enters the id scan only at a `[` byte after the trailer branch declines, so a proposition naming another claim in running prose is silently missed — and this memo's own C13 concedes exactly that. The concession is not a footnote to the error direction, it inverts it: for scheduling, a missed edge is precisely silent under-grading, the failure mode this claim says cannot occur. Measured on the corpus: across 90 claims in the five rendered memos there are zero bracketed citation-shaped ids inside any proposition and four bare prose references, one of them in this memo's own C4 ("the same grandfathering C5 turns on"). So on the observed population the matcher's error direction for rule 5 is false negatives only, not false positives only.

The replacement matcher is specified as "a whitespace- or punctuation-delimited token in a proposition is an edge when it is byte-equal to an id that this document's ledger defines". A hyphen is punctuation, so on any ledger whose ids contain one that tokenisation can never produce a token byte-equal to an id, and the closure yields the empty edge set — the exact defect the claim uses to reject `citation_ids_in`, moved onto a different population. That population is not hypothetical: src/citations.rs 38-55 states the id shape as uppercase-led "with a digit or a hyphen" and names `S3-L17`, `E-4`, `X-6`, `R-ROOT`, `CYC-A` as corpus-ledger ids, two of them "real ids in this crate's own fixtures"; the captured rg sweep returns 21 hyphenated ledger row ids across nine fixture documents and two source modules, with no unhyphenated one among them. Worse for the comparison the claim draws, src/ledger.rs 361-383 — the importer's well-formed-row test — has claim `X-1` with proposition "`foo` returns **4** always [X-2]": a bracketed citation-shaped sibling id inside a proposition, which `citation_ids_in` (src/citations.rs 84-120) does find and the ledger-membership matcher as worded does not. The "not one proposition contains a bracketed citation-shaped id" measurement was taken over the five rendered memos only, so it does not reach the imported-ledger documents this crate also checks, and on those the two matchers' merits are reversed. The claim holds as written only for ledgers whose ids are alphanumeric throughout, i.e. tetel-minted `C\d+`; it needs either a tokenisation that admits the crate's own id characters (alphanumeric, `_`, `-`, as scan_line already does inside brackets) or an explicit restriction of rule 5 to alphanumeric-id ledgers.

Everything but one number holds. Over the four other rendered memos in docs/design I replayed the corpus with the shipped `brief --json`: zero propositions of 61 contain a bracketed citation-shaped token, and real unbracketed same-ledger references exist in tet30 (C3 names C9 and C13). The clause that does not survive is the corpus size: "all five rendered memos — 90 claims". docs/design holds exactly five rendered memos, four of which carry 15+14+13+19 = 61 claims, and the fifth's own grounding brief announces 32 claims — 93, not 90. The figure looks measured against an earlier state of the fifth ledger (its ids run to C34 with two withdrawn). The qualitative findings the closure decision rests on are unaffected; the count is stale.

records.prop: Rule 5's matching rule should be the crate's existing `citation_ids_in` rather than a new `C\d+` scan: the existing matcher is already the definition of a row→row citation edge for the dependency-cascade check, it is id-shape-agnostic (a `C\d+` regex would miss real ids of the `R-ROOT` / `CYC-A` shape the crate's own fixtures use, a genuine false-negative class), and its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading.
verdicts: "Its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading" holds only under a condition the claim does not state: that every inter-claim reference an author writes inside a proposition is bracketed or sits in a whole-line cites trailer. It is not. `scan_line` (src/citations.rs 55-140) enters the id scan only at a `[` byte after the trailer branch declines, so a proposition naming another claim in running prose is silently missed — and this memo's own C13 concedes exactly that. The concession is not a footnote to the error direction, it inverts it: for scheduling, a missed edge is precisely silent under-grading, the failure mode this claim says cannot occur. Measured on the corpus: across 90 claims in the five rendered memos there are zero bracketed citation-shaped ids inside any proposition and four bare prose references, one of them in this memo's own C4 ("the same grandfathering C5 turns on"). So on the observed population the matcher's error direction for rule 5 is false negatives only, not false positives only.

The replacement matcher is specified as "a whitespace- or punctuation-delimited token in a proposition is an edge when it is byte-equal to an id that this document's ledger defines". A hyphen is punctuation, so on any ledger whose ids contain one that tokenisation can never produce a token byte-equal to an id, and the closure yields the empty edge set — the exact defect the claim uses to reject `citation_ids_in`, moved onto a different population. That population is not hypothetical: src/citations.rs 38-55 states the id shape as uppercase-led "with a digit or a hyphen" and names `S3-L17`, `E-4`, `X-6`, `R-ROOT`, `CYC-A` as corpus-ledger ids, two of them "real ids in this crate's own fixtures"; the captured rg sweep returns 21 hyphenated ledger row ids across nine fixture documents and two source modules, with no unhyphenated one among them. The "not one proposition contains a bracketed citation-shaped id" measurement was taken over the five rendered memos only, so it does not reach the imported-ledger documents this crate also checks, and on those the two matchers' merits are reversed. The claim holds as written only for ledgers whose ids are alphanumeric throughout, i.e. tetel-minted `C\d+`; it needs either a tokenisation that admits the crate's own id characters (alphanumeric, `_`, `-`, as scan_line already does inside brackets) or an explicit restriction of rule 5 to alphanumeric-id ledgers.

That branch cannot rescue a proposition that merely names a claim in ordinary prose (the trailer must be the entire trimmed line), so the residual false negative stands as described; only the "only at a `[` byte" mechanism clause is inexact. Separately, `is_citation_shaped` also requires an id to contain a digit or a hyphen, so a bracketed id of a shape with neither would be a second, narrower residual miss.
