records.prop: There should be no `--owed` flag: because the full brief is emitted either way, an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve, while TET-46's stated objection to a flag — that it "leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call" — applies with more force to a brief, the one artifact independence rests on, since two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents; the confirmation floor stays a parameter, and the value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact.
verdicts: The no-flag decision stands; its closing remedy does not reach one of the two surfaces. "The value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact" is met only for the text brief. `brief` already emits two documents from one memo depending on a flag the caller types: src/lib.rs 186-217 dispatches on `json` between `render_text` and `render_json` (src/brief.rs 36 and 62), reached by `--json` in src/main.rs 28-60 and main.rs:351. Since the design's own target list (C19) puts the owed section and the floor value in `render_text` only, a pass that runs `brief --json` receives a brief with neither — reinstating exactly the property this claim rejects a flag for, that the configuration leaves no trace in the artifact, and additionally making the two passes' briefs differ in content rather than in encoding. Also, this claim's premise that "two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents" is already true of `--json` today; the argument needs the stronger form that they must not receive different *content*, which is what the render_json omission breaks.
The TET-46 quotation is exact and correctly attributed as its objection to a flag.

"The full brief is emitted either way" rests on `build`'s unconditional one-for-one map and its doc comment forbidding any drop; and the two renderers are the two places a floor value would have to be printed, since neither prints any parameter today.

The TET-46 objection is quoted byte-exactly, including the "no flag" conclusion it supports. The rest of the proposition — that the full brief is emitted either way and no prior behaviour would be preserved by a flag, and that the floor stays a parameter printed by both renderers — rests on `build`'s unconditional map and the two-renderer shape I recorded separately; the printing requirement is a prescription, not yet code.

TET-46's objection is quoted accurately — docs/design/tet46-look-never-returns-tetel-content.md:85 reads "A flag would add a fourth route with a property none of these has — it leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call." That the full brief is emitted either way, so an owed section is purely additive with no prior behaviour to preserve, follows from `build`'s unconditional one-for-one mapping and its doc.

"Purely additive" is true only in the sense of removal, and the claim spends it in the stronger sense. The no-flag argument rests on "an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve". There is prior behaviour: today's brief is evidence-blind by construction. `build` takes `&[Claim]` only and neither renderer emits a field derived from the evidence ledger, and brief.rs's module doc states this shape is a confidentiality device — scope is withheld "so an independent grounding pass can't see what the author declared", "enforced by its shape, not by care at render time" (F2). tests/brief_cli.rs states the reciprocal contract for evidence state in its own words: `brief` "must keep listing it exactly as if nothing had been recorded yet, until a witnessed grounding lands" (F3). An owed list is the first evidence-derived channel into that artifact: a grounder handed one learns, per claim, whether at least N independent workspaces have already graded the wording it is about to grade. That is prior behaviour a flag would preserve, and it is disclosure into the one artifact C16 itself calls "the one artifact independence rests on". The no-flag conclusion may still be right, but not on the ground that nothing is being given up.

The quoted objection is byte-exact against TET-46's prose at line 85 of that memo. Combined with brief.rs — where build emits every claim unconditionally and both renderers already print the whole list — the "no prior behaviour a flag would preserve" premise holds, and the reasoning that two passes must not receive different briefs is the same objection applied to the artifact independence rests on.

The no-flag decision holds only under a condition the claim does not state: that N is constrained to at least 1. C16 rejects `--owed` on the ground that "two passes running `brief` on the same memo must not receive different documents", then accepts the floor as a caller-supplied parameter. C24 states the predicate as an unqualified "owed iff fewer than N ..." with no lower bound, and C31 gives N a default without an admissible range. At N=0 no claim is ever owed on any memo — the owed section is empty — which is exactly the document a `--owed`-off flag would produce. So `brief --confirm 0` reinstates through the accepted parameter the artifact the claim rejects as a flag, and two passes at N=0 and N=2 do receive different documents from one memo. C28's separating argument ("a schedule and never a settlement") applies word for word to the flag, so it does not distinguish the two; and C16's other ground, TET-46's no-trace objection, is cured for N by printing the floor in force, a remedy that would equally cure it for the flag. The decision is defensible with "N >= 1" written into the predicate and rejected at both front ends; as the claim stands, that constraint is asserted nowhere in the ledger and assigned to nobody in the Modification targets table.

Everything but one clause holds: build takes &[Claim] alone (F4), build's own doc forbids dropping a claim on account of its evidence ledger, tests/brief_cli.rs carries the quoted sentence and asserts the ingested-only claim is still listed (F12), and TET-46's quoted sentence is verbatim at tet46 line 85 (F13). The clause I cannot support as written is "its module doc calls that shape a confidentiality device enforced by shape rather than by care", where "that shape" is `build` taking `&[Claim]` alone. The module doc's shape-enforcement sentence is attached to a different thing and to a different property: "`BriefItem` carries no field a scope could leak through — that's enforced by its shape, not by care at render time." That is about BriefItem's field list and about scope leakage, not about build's parameter list or about evidence-blindness. The evidence-blindness contract is stated in the code, but by build's own doc comment, not by the module doc's shape sentence.

The TET-46 quotation is byte-exact at that memo's line 85. The other checkable clauses hold too: build takes &[Claim] alone and its doc forbids dropping a claim on evidence grounds, the module doc's "enforced by its shape, not by care at render time" sentence is about BriefItem's field list and scope (F2), and brief_cli.rs carries the quoted "must keep listing it exactly as if nothing had been recorded yet, until a witnessed grounding lands" (F7). The N>=1 rejection is a design decision, not a code fact.

records.prop: Rule 4's visibility requirement is met by extending the existing per-claim provenance line in `grounding_provenance` with the number of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the claim's current wording, printed as a bullet in the human-owed partition exactly as that line already is; `check` states the count and never compares it against a floor, because the floor is `brief`'s parameter and a comparison printed by `check` would be a per-claim verdict on a policy setting rather than a count of records.
verdicts: "The existing per-claim provenance line" is three different emission states, and the extension reaches only one of them — the one where the count is least likely to be zero. src/checks.rs 972-1050: when a claim has no evidence records at all, `grounding_provenance` does `continue` and emits NO line; when the witnessed subset is empty, it emits a different string ("grounded, all N record(s) ingested — extent typed by the reporter...") that carries no workspace list and no counts; only the third branch emits the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) ..." line the claim proposes to extend, and the by_author/by_others split it would extend exists only inside `AuthoringIdentity::Known`. So a reader gets the new count exactly when a claim already has at least one witnessed record, and gets nothing where the count would be 0 — precisely the claims rule 4 schedules. The visibility requirement is met for grounded-and-witnessed claims only; the claim as written says it is met, without that condition. The rest of the claim — that `check` states the count and never compares it to N — is unaffected.

The mechanical half is confirmed: the provenance line is already emitted per grounded claim and already printed as a `  - ` bullet in report.rs's human-owed partition, so extending that same string with a count reaches the reader exactly as the proposition says. What I cannot establish from source is the normative half — that this "meets" rule 4's visibility requirement, and that `check` should state the count without comparing it to a floor. That is a design decision about a surface that does not exist yet; there is no code that states or fails to state it. Graded on the code half only.

The three-way split is correct on the axis it enumerates and incomplete on a second, independent one. src/checks.rs 940-1060: the outer branch is indeed three-way over record composition (no records -> `continue`; no witnessed records -> the all-ingested string; else the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)" line). But inside the third branch `standing` switches on `AuthoringIdentity`, and `by_author`/`by_others` are computed only in the `Known(author)` arm — under `NoSnapshot` and `SnapshotWithoutIdentity` the function emits "cannot be determined from here" because there is no author to subtract. So "the count of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the wording a claim carries now" has no value to print in two of the three identity modes, and the instruction "It goes in all three" does not say what is emitted there. This is the same pair of states C10 keys the floor on, so it is not an edge case the design ignores elsewhere: C10 decides that in those states every claim is owed under rule 4, and C17 needs a matching decision about what the visibility line says — a count is not computable, and printing a bare zero would read as "no independent pass has graded this" when the truth is "nothing here can tell". Separately, emitting the count in the first branch means `grounding_provenance` now emits a line for claims with no evidence at all, which its own field doc describes as "one line per grounded claim" and which `analyze_ledger` already reports as ungrounded; the design should say whether that duplication is intended.

The "printed in the human-owed partition as its lines already are" clause: report.rs's loop over findings.grounding_provenance sits inside the human-owed block beside superseded_evidence and qualified_claims, one "  - {line}" per entry, never contributing to a failure.

The descriptive half is exact: the three composition states (no records → `continue`, emits nothing; all-ingested → a string with no workspace list; witnessed → the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)" line), and within the third a second branch on AuthoringIdentity where a non-author count (`by_others`) is computed only in the `Known` arm, with NoSnapshot and SnapshotWithoutIdentity producing "cannot be determined from here" and no count. The remaining sentences are prescriptions for code that does not exist yet, so they are design decisions rather than facts of the tree; nothing I read contradicts them.

The description of the branching is exact — I read src/checks.rs 972-1050 and the three composition states and the `AuthoringIdentity` sub-branch are as stated, with `by_author`/`by_others` existing only in the `Known` arm. What does not hold is the completeness the proposition asserts for the purpose it uses the enumeration for: "the function branches on two axes, not one." There is a third, and it is the axis this design itself introduces. Every set the function builds — `records`, `witnessed`, `passes`, `by_author`, `by_others` — is selected by `claim_id` alone; `proposition_digest` is never read anywhere in the function. C9 requires the floor's count to be restricted to records matching the current wording, so the count and the sentence it is appended to would be computed over different record sets. Constructed case: a claim whose three witnessed records all graded a superseded wording, from three non-author workspaces. It lands in the third composition state, so the line prints "grounded, 3 of 3 record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) A, B, C — independently grounded: no grounding workspace here is the one that authored this memo", while the digest-restricted count appended to that same line is 0 and rule 4 schedules the claim. The `(0, _)` and `(_, 0)` arms produce "independently grounded" and "SELF-GROUNDED" from the unrestricted `passes` vector, so the standing verdict and the new count contradict each other on one line about one claim. This is the same trap one layer down from the one the claim credits itself with catching, and placing the count correctly requires the digest axis to be in the enumeration. Second, smaller: the instruction to emit the count in the first composition state turns a bare `continue` into a bullet for every claim with no evidence record — the population src/report.rs 179-200 already covers under "ungrounded ledger claims" in the same flat bullet list, so that state yields two bullets per claim, 32 of them on this memo's current ledger.

The two-axis structure is exactly as described. Composition axis: `records.is_empty()` continues without emitting; `witnessed.is_empty()` emits the all-ingested string with no workspace list; only the third branch carries "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)". Identity axis inside that third branch: `by_others` is computed only in the `Known(author)` arm, and the `NoSnapshot`/`SnapshotWithoutIdentity` arms produce a "cannot be determined from here" string with no count at all. src/report.rs:198 prints each of these lines verbatim as a bullet in the human-owed partition, which the section header says is "none of this is settled by a passing check", so the prescription that `check` state a count without comparing it to a floor is consistent with where the lines already land.

The two branch axes the claim enumerates are real and correctly described, and it misses a third that defeats the visibility requirement it is discharging. Inside `AuthoringIdentity::Known`, `grounding_provenance` branches again on `(by_author, by_others)` into three arms emitting three different verdict words — "independently grounded" at (0,_), "SELF-GROUNDED" at (_,0), "MIXED: {a} ... {o}" otherwise. All three are computed over `passes`, deduped from `witnessed` with NO digest filter, which is exactly the restriction C9 says the floor must add and this function does not have. So the claim's remedy puts a digest-AWARE count next to a digest-BLIND verdict word on the same line, and does not require the word to change. Measured on this memo: the design's own third disjunct yields 0 distinct non-author witnessed passes on the current wording for all 28 claims (digest method validated — my sha256 over C15's brief proposition reproduces the current digest `check` prints, ba2c43a63cb9), while the same `check` run prints "C35: grounded, 1 of 1 record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) 5e0280207036a210 — independently grounded", and likewise for C36, C33 and C32. A reader of that line is told a claim is independently grounded in the same breath as being told its confirmation count is zero. Appending the count does not meet the visibility requirement; making the verdict word digest-aware, or moving the count off that line, would.

All three branching axes are exactly as described: composition (empty records -> continue; witnessed empty -> ingested string with no workspace list; else the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)" line), identity (non-author count only in the Known arm), and (by_author, by_others) into "independently grounded"/"SELF-GROUNDED"/"MIXED" — all over passes deduped from witnessed records with no digest filter, so the stated collision between a digest-restricted count of zero and the phrase "independently grounded" is real.

The diagnosis is exact and the prescribed remedy does not clear the trap it names. C17 correctly identifies that appending a digest-restricted count without restricting the words "puts a count of zero beside the phrase 'independently grounded' on one line", and instructs: "the words must be computed over the same digest-restricted set as the count". The innermost branch is `match (by_author, by_others) { (0, _) => "independently grounded...", (_, 0) => "SELF-GROUNDED...", (a, o) => "MIXED..." }` with no arm for the empty case (F4). Restrict `passes` to digest-matching records and, for exactly the claims the floor schedules, the set is empty, so `(0, 0)` matches the first arm and the line still reads "independently grounded: no grounding workspace here is the one that authored this memo" — now beside a zero count and an empty `passes.join(", ")` workspace list. records.prop: Rule 4's visibility requirement is met by extending the existing per-claim provenance line in `grounding_provenance` with the number of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the claim's current wording, printed as a bullet in the human-owed partition exactly as that line already is; `check` states the count and never compares it against a floor, because the floor is `brief`'s parameter and a comparison printed by `check` would be a per-claim verdict on a policy setting rather than a count of records.
verdicts: "The existing per-claim provenance line" is three different emission states, and the extension reaches only one of them — the one where the count is least likely to be zero. src/checks.rs 972-1050: when a claim has no evidence records at all, `grounding_provenance` does `continue` and emits NO line; when the witnessed subset is empty, it emits a different string ("grounded, all N record(s) ingested — extent typed by the reporter...") that carries no workspace list and no counts; only the third branch emits the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) ..." line the claim proposes to extend, and the by_author/by_others split it would extend exists only inside `AuthoringIdentity::Known`. So a reader gets the new count exactly when a claim already has at least one witnessed record, and gets nothing where the count would be 0 — precisely the claims rule 4 schedules. The visibility requirement is met for grounded-and-witnessed claims only; the claim as written says it is met, without that condition. The rest of the claim — that `check` states the count and never compares it to N — is unaffected.

The mechanical half is confirmed: the provenance line is already emitted per grounded claim and already printed as a `  - ` bullet in report.rs's human-owed partition, so extending that same string with a count reaches the reader exactly as the proposition says. What I cannot establish from source is the normative half — that this "meets" rule 4's visibility requirement, and that `check` should state the count without comparing it to a floor. That is a design decision about a surface that does not exist yet; there is no code that states or fails to state it. Graded on the code half only.

The three-way split is correct on the axis it enumerates and incomplete on a second, independent one. src/checks.rs 940-1060: the outer branch is indeed three-way over record composition (no records -> `continue`; no witnessed records -> the all-ingested string; else the "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)" line). But inside the third branch `standing` switches on `AuthoringIdentity`, and `by_author`/`by_others` are computed only in the `Known(author)` arm — under `NoSnapshot` and `SnapshotWithoutIdentity` the function emits "cannot be determined from here" because there is no author to subtract. So "the count of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the wording a claim carries now" has no value to print in two of the three identity modes, and the instruction "It goes in all three" does not say what is emitted there. This is the same pair of states C10 keys the floor on, so it is not an edge case the design ignores elsewhere: C10 decides that in those states every claim is owed under rule 4, and C17 needs a matching decision about what the visibility line says — a count is not computable, and printing a bare zero would read as "no independent pass has graded this" when the truth is "nothing here can tell". Separately, emitting the count in the first branch means `grounding_provenance` now emits a line for claims with no evidence at all, which its own field doc describes as "one line per grounded claim" and which `analyze_ledger` already reports as ungrounded; the design should say whether that duplication is intended.

The "printed in the human-owed partition as its lines already are" clause: report.rs's loop over findings.grounding_provenance sits inside the human-owed block beside superseded_evidence and qualified_claims, one "  - {line}" per entry, never contributing to a failure.

The remaining sentences are prescriptions for code that does not exist yet, so they are design decisions rather than facts of the tree; nothing I read contradicts them.

What does not hold is the completeness the proposition asserts for the purpose it uses the enumeration for: "the function branches on two axes, not one." There is a third, and it is the axis this design itself introduces. Every set the function builds — `records`, `witnessed`, `passes`, `by_author`, `by_others` — is selected by `claim_id` alone; `proposition_digest` is never read anywhere in the function. C9 requires the floor's count to be restricted to records matching the current wording, so the count and the sentence it is appended to would be computed over different record sets. Constructed case: a claim whose three witnessed records all graded a superseded wording, from three non-author workspaces. It lands in the third composition state, so the line prints "grounded, 3 of 3 record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) A, B, C — independently grounded: no grounding workspace here is the one that authored this memo", while the digest-restricted count appended to that same line is 0 and rule 4 schedules the claim. The `(0, _)` and `(_, 0)` arms produce "independently grounded" and "SELF-GROUNDED" from the unrestricted `passes` vector, so the standing verdict and the new count contradict each other on one line about one claim. This is the same trap one layer down from the one the claim credits itself with catching, and placing the count correctly requires the digest axis to be in the enumeration. The two-axis structure is exactly as described. Composition axis: `records.is_empty()` continues without emitting; `witnessed.is_empty()` emits the all-ingested string with no workspace list; only the third branch carries "N of M record(s) witnessed in workspace(s)". The two branch axes the claim enumerates are real and correctly described, and it misses a third that defeats the visibility requirement it is discharging. Inside `AuthoringIdentity::Known`, `grounding_provenance` branches again on `(by_author, by_others)` into three arms emitting three different verdict words — "independently grounded" at (0,_), "SELF-GROUNDED" at (_,0), "MIXED: {a} ... {o}" otherwise. All three are computed over `passes`, deduped from `witnessed` with NO digest filter, which is exactly the restriction C9 says the floor must add and this function does not have. So the claim's remedy puts a digest-AWARE count next to a digest-BLIND verdict word on the same line, and does not require the word to change. Measured on this memo: the design's own third disjunct yields 0 distinct non-author witnessed passes on the current wording for all 28 claims (digest method validated — my sha256 over C15's brief proposition reproduces the current digest `check` prints, ba2c43a63cb9), while the same `check` run prints "C35: grounded, 1 of 1 record(s) witnessed in workspace(s) 5e0280207036a210 — independently grounded", and likewise for C36, C33 and C32. A reader of that line is told a claim is independently grounded in the same breath as being told its confirmation count is zero. Appending the count does not meet the visibility requirement; making the verdict word digest-aware, or moving the count off that line, would.

records.prop: Extending the per-claim provenance line reaches exactly three files: `grounding_provenance` is named only in src/checks.rs (its field, its zero-init, its definition), src/lib.rs (its single call site) and src/report.rs (the loop printing its strings), with no test or fixture depending on its wording, so the change has one producer and one consumer.
verdicts: The symbol census is exact — `grounding_provenance` is named on 7 lines in precisely checks.rs (doc ref, field, zero-init, definition), lib.rs (one call site) and report.rs (one printing loop), and one producer / one consumer is right. The false clause is "with no test or fixture depending on its wording". Grepping the emitted strings rather than the identifier turns up five end-to-end tests in tests/authoring_cli.rs asserting on the text of these very lines — "all 1 record(s) ingested", "not captured by this tool", "SELF-GROUNDED", "no independent pass has run", "independently grounded", "MIXED", "not as independent confirmation", "cannot be determined from here" — plus one further hit under tests/ asserting the negation of the last. They are substring assertions, so appending a count would probably survive them, but "no test depends on its wording" is not true, and the change therefore reaches a fourth file's worth of expectations that a census by identifier alone does not show.

The three-file identifier reach is confirmed (checks.rs, lib.rs's single call site, report.rs's printing loop, no test naming the identifier), and both named string dependents exist as stated: authoring_cli.rs:1028/1083 assert `SELF-GROUNDED` and `cannot be determined from here`, mcp_cli.rs:820 asserts the absence of the latter, all as `String::contains` substring tests. I also found two further substring assertions the memo does not name — authoring_cli.rs:944 and :973 on "1 of 1 record(s) witnessed" and "1 of 2 record(s) witnessed" — which strengthen rather than contradict the point, since they too sit on the very line a count would be appended to and would also survive an append.

The two named test files assert exactly the described strings, as substring contains() on the check report rather than by identifier, so an appended count would leave them passing — matching the claim's "likely to leave them passing".

verdicts: One provenance detail worth naming: the quoted phrase "never reported as its own dependent" is the comment on the `visited.insert(root.id)` seeding, while the self-edge skip carries its own comment "self-citation is not a dependency". records.prop: On the same replay, a rule with no confirmation floor — one workspace-grading per wording — would have retained none of the seven discoveries while cutting workspace-gradings from 69 to 35; N=2 retains five of seven at 51 gradings (a 26% reduction, slightly less than the ticket's estimated 28%), N=3 retains six at 60, and N=4 retains all seven at 67. The floor is therefore what carries the discovery property, and the saving is bought against it monotonically.
verdicts: Every number reproduces on an independent re-run (35/51/60/67 gradings, 0/5/6/7 discoveries), but the one the design leans hardest on carries no information. A "discovery" is defined in this replay as a cross-workspace regrade giving a verdict no EARLIER workspace gave, so its ordinal is at least 2 for any ledger that could ever be replayed; the observed ordinals are [2,2,2,2,2,3,4]. Capping at one workspace per wording therefore retains zero discoveries by identity, on this ledger and on every other, including one where a floor would be worthless. So "a rule with no confirmation floor would have retained none of the seven" does not measure the floor's necessity — it restates the definition. Likewise N=4 retaining all seven is fixed by the maximum observed ordinal being 4. The empirical content of the replay is the ordinal distribution and the cost curve, and that content supports the weaker and still-useful proposition the memo could have made: five of the seven arrive at the second workspace, so N=2 buys 5/7 for 16 extra gradings. The sentence "the floor is therefore what carries the discovery property" is the one that spends the definitional figure as though it were an observation. Context worth stating: only 16 of the 35 pairs were ever graded by two or more distinct workspaces at all.

Every figure reproduces on an independent replay of tet30's ledger: 35 (claim, digest) pairs, 69 unbounded workspace-gradings, 7 discoveries at ordinals 5/1/1, the curve 35/51/60/67 at N=1..4, and N=2 buying five of the seven for sixteen gradings above the dirty-only floor. The final clause does not hold. "Each further N buys less" is false at the step this design's default turns on: N=2->N=3 costs 9 gradings for 1 discovery, N=3->N=4 costs 7 gradings for the last 1. The marginal price per discovery falls from nine to seven, so returns are not monotonically diminishing in cost, and the run also shows N=4 retaining all seven discoveries at 67 of the 69 gradings full re-grading performs — a cap at 4 forgoes nothing and saves two. The prose at memo line 11, "every further step buys less for more", carries the same error. This matters because that monotonicity is the stated reason for stopping low; the measured curve supports a floor over no floor, and supports 2 over 1, but does not support 2 over 3 or 4 by diminishing returns.

Cost curve reproduced: 35, 51, 60, 67 at N=1..4 against 69 unbounded, so N=2 is 16 gradings above the dirty-only floor and captures 5 of 7. The analytic point holds too — a discovery is defined as a verdict no earlier workspace gave, so its ordinal is at least 2 on any ledger and "a floor of 1 retains nothing" is entailed rather than measured. The only looseness is "each further N buys less": the marginal buys are 5, then 1, then 1, so the last two steps buy equally, though each costs less than the first per unit of schedule. Not enough to withhold support.

The cost curve reproduces: 35/51/60/67 at N=1..4 against 69 unbounded, with marginal steps 9 (2 to 3, buying the one ordinal-3 discovery) and 7 (3 to 4, buying the ordinal-4 one), so the per-discovery price falls rather than rises. Seven verdict changes did occur and five arrived from the second workspace to read a wording. The claim that a floor of 1 retaining nothing is entailed rather than measured is correct: a discovery is defined as a verdict no earlier workspace gave, so its ordinal is at least 2 by construction. The "only floor at which the feature saves materially" judgement is stated over floors that retain any discovery at all (N=1 saves 34 but retains none by definition), and the proposition itself supplies that framing.

Cost curve reproduces exactly: 35, 51, 60, 67 at N=1..4 against 69 unbounded. Seven verdict changes occurred, five from the second workspace to read a wording. The 2->3 step costs 9 gradings for one discovery and 3->4 costs 7 for the last, so the marginal price falls rather than rises, as stated. That a floor of 1 retains nothing is indeed entailed — a discovery's ordinal is >= 2 by its own definition — and my replay confirms it empirically too.

Cost curve 35/51/60/67 against 69 unbounded reproduces exactly; seven verdict changes occurred, five from the second workspace to read a wording; marginal steps are 9 gradings for one discovery (2 to 3) and 7 for the last (3 to 4), so the price per discovery falls rather than rises. That N=1 retains nothing is indeed entailed: a discovery is defined as a verdict no earlier workspace gave, so its ordinal is at least 2 by construction, which the replay's ordinals (all >= 2) exhibit.

Every numeric clause reproduces — 7 verdict changes, 5 from the second workspace, the cost curve 35/51/60/67 against 69, and the marginal steps of 9 then 7 gradings per discovery, so "the marginal price does not rise with N" holds. The final clause does not follow from the replay: "it is the only floor at which the feature saves materially at all" is an evaluative judgement, and the same numbers show N=3 saving 9 gradings of 69 (13%) against N=2's 18 (26%) — a difference of degree, not the presence or absence of a saving. C31 in this same ledger declines to settle exactly that judgement ("whether 9 gradings is worth the sixth discovery is a judgement the replay does not settle"), and C31's own phrasing is the weaker "not because it is the only floor that saves anything".

records.prop: The owed predicate as decided here: a claim is owed iff it is in `analyze_ledger`'s `ungrounded_claims`, or in its `out_of_proof`, or the pin stored on its records differs from the memo's currently stated pin, or fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have a record whose `proposition_digest` equals the current proposition's, or `citation_ids_in` finds in its proposition text the id of a claim that is itself owed — the last computed to a fixpoint. Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot, and each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes.
verdicts: The third disjunct of the decided predicate is not well defined, on two counts, and the claim's closing sentence ("each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes") does not hold for it. (a) "The pin stored on its records" is written as a single value; it is not. Replay of tet30's ledger: 125 records, 61 distinct pin values in that one file, and all 13 claims carry records with more than one distinct pin — C11 has 16, C10 and C12 have 8 each. Four of the five disjuncts hold as stated and the closing summary is right for them. The third disjunct is not: "the pin stored on its records" is, on the witnessed path, `Some(fact.pin.clone())`, and a Fact's pin is `sha256:` + a hash over each extent entry's label, world_root, world_state and output (src/facts.rs:414-436) — never a VCS revision, whereas "the memo's currently stated pin" is a git hash parsed out of prose by `find_stated_pin` (the crate's own tests assert `abc1234` and `deadbee`). Compared directly, the two can never be equal, so this disjunct fires unconditionally on every witnessed-grounded claim rather than detecting a re-pin; the field that actually records the tree an observation was taken against is `world: Vec<worldstate::Marker>`, not `pin`. The final sentence is also over-broad on that disjunct: "each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes" is true of rule 1 (`ungrounded_claims`), rule 2 (`out_of_proof`) and rule 4 (`by_others` inside `grounding_provenance`), but not of rule 3 — no check in the crate reads a record's pin at all (F5), so there is no computed set to reuse. "Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot" is true as written (F7).

Three qualifications on the predicate as decided. (1) Disjunct 3 is not merely "not a reuse", it is permanently true for any memo whose worktree has moved since authoring — four of the five memos in this corpus are already in that state today (see the refutation recorded against C27 from the same fact), so for them the predicate degenerates to "every claim is owed" and the saving the design exists for is zero. (2) Disjunct 4 as worded says "fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have a record whose proposition_digest equals the current proposition's" — it does not say witnessed. On the ingested path `RecordInput.pass` is caller-supplied free text (src/evidence.rs 150-240), against which the witnessed path's own comment reads "The pass *is* the workspace. Not a name someone chose", and `world` is written empty by construction. So the disjunct as stated is dischargeable by N `record --input` calls with N made-up `pass` strings, none of which is a workspace and none of which is non-author in any checkable sense — the self-attestation the floor exists to prevent. C9 supplies a mechanism (`by_others`, witnessed-only) that has no such hole, but C24 is the sentence an implementer builds from and it is strictly weaker than the mechanism it cites. (3) "Four of the five reuse a computation the crate already performs" is qualified for rule 4: `fresh` is a function-local in `analyze_ledger` and `LedgerFindings` (src/checks.rs 150-200) exposes no such set, so counting `fresh` records per C5 means recomputing `sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` and the digest comparison inside `grounding_provenance` — a second definition of "graded on this wording", which is the drift C4 says the design avoids by taking rules 1 and 2 from analyze_ledger's outputs.

Three of the four disjuncts are as decided; the third's stated justification holds only under an unstated condition. "'Witnessed' is load-bearing ... a floor counting ingested passes would be dischargeable by inventing names, whereas on the witnessed path the pass is the workspace identity" draws a contrast the code does not support. src/workspace.rs 95-175: a workspace identity is created on first use of a caller-chosen workspace name, seeded from the workspace directory path, birth time, pid and nanoseconds, and the doc states "an independent grounding pass is simply *defined* as a fresh workspace" while the inline comment states "Uniqueness, not unpredictability: this names a workspace, it does not authenticate one. Nothing here resists a determined forger." So the witnessed path is also dischargeable by inventing names — one agent passing N different `workspace` strings in one session yields N distinct passes. The real difference is weaker and worth stating in the claim: the witnessed path forces each of those workspaces to have captured its own observations, so the floor counts distinct capture efforts, not distinct readers. The discovery property the floor exists to preserve (C23) was measured over passes assumed independent; the rule as decided cannot tell N independent readers from one reader with N workspace names, and nothing in the predicate closes that.

records.prop: The textual closure needs no author-side claim-to-claim dependency edge: its edges are read out of proposition text by `citation_ids_in` at schedule time, from artifacts the memo carries, so grounding scheduling is computable without the re-evaluation obligation the ticket puts out of scope.
verdicts: `citation_ids_in` reads edges out of arbitrary text at call time and is already the crate's row→row edge definition, so no stored author-side claim-to-claim edge is required. The reference to what "the ticket puts out of scope" is not checkable from the pinned repository, but nothing in the claim's operative assertion depends on it.

The proposition states that the closure's "edges are read out of proposition text by `citation_ids_in` at schedule time". That is the mechanism this memo's own C12 rejects: C12 states that a closure built on `citation_ids_in` "yields the empty edge set on every memo in the corpus", and the decided matcher is instead membership in the document's own ledger. The memo's own F10 row records that `scan_line` "only enters the id scan at a `[` byte", so `citation_ids_in` does not see the unbracketed sibling references C12 says are the only real ones. C26 is therefore false as written about the design as decided, and it is not a harmless wording slip: it and the paragraph citing it (memo line 157, "the same scanner the cascade already uses") are the only place the memo tells an implementer *what* reads the edges, so a reader who builds C26 builds the closure C12 measured as firing on nothing. The proposition's other half — that no author-side claim-to-claim dependency graph is needed — survives under the ledger-membership matcher, so the fix is to restate the mechanism, not to drop the claim.

The named mechanism is wrong. `citation_ids_in` is `scan_line`, a pure shape test that recognises only inline `[ID]`/`[!ID]` passing `is_citation_shaped` and a whole-line `*cites: ...*` trailer; it consults no ledger and matches nothing unbracketed. Edges "read out of proposition text by `citation_ids_in`" are therefore the empty set on any proposition without bracketed citation syntax.

Empirically the same point: across the four other rendered memos, zero of 61 propositions contain a bracketed citation-shaped token, so a closure whose edges are read by `citation_ids_in` has no edges at all on this corpus. The conclusion C26 draws — that no author-side claim-to-claim edge is needed — may well survive under the ledger-id-membership matcher the design settles on elsewhere, but not by the mechanism this proposition names.

records.prop: In `look_grep` the author-facing return (`printed`) and the captured evidence (the pending buffer entries) are built separately from the same grep stdout, so a bound applied while assembling `printed` leaves the `Search` and `GrepMatch` entries — and therefore the extent, the pin and the snapshot — byte-identical to today's.
verdicts: In look_grep, `printed` is a distinct `String::new()` (observe.rs:418) that receives `stdout` by borrow via push_str, while the `Search` entry (output empty) and the `GrepMatch` entries (output built from `stdout.lines()` via by_file) are assembled independently from the same `stdout`. Nothing reads `printed` back, so bounding it cannot alter the entries, their labels, or their keys.

True of the bound in isolation; false of the design, and the prose spends the unqualified form. `facts::mint` computes the pin as sha256 over, for every pending entry, `label` + `world_root` + `world_state` + `output` (facts.rs:417-435, its own comment: "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker"), and copies `label` into the fact's extent (facts.rs:400-411). C17 requires the `Search` label to gain a "showed N of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound)" segment, and C20 requires the same of the `look_path` label. So for any observation on which the bound bites, the extent bytes change, the pin changes, and the snapshot's facts.jsonl changes — the exact three things this claim says stay byte-identical to today's, and on which the memo rests "what makes f3 cheap and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope". F2 shows the crate already reasons this way: the test comment at authoring_cli.rs:508-510 justifies naming memos in the label precisely so that two differently-excluded searches "would not pin identically".

The second half is the implementer-facing bite. This claim's mechanism is that `printed` and the pending entries "are built separately... neither reads the other" — today true, and F1(5) confirms the `Search` label is computed from `root`, `pattern`, `by_file.len()` and `note`, none of which touch `printed`. After the change the label must carry N, a number that exists only as a product of bounding `printed`. The design therefore creates the coupling this claim says is absent, and an implementer who took the claim at face value ("a bound imposed while assembling `printed` cannot reach the buffer") would bound `printed` and leave the label alone — which is the design's own defect back again.

What survives unqualified: the captured `output`, the key and the world markers do stay byte-identical, so overlap and re-resolvability are untouched (F1(2),(3): `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads kind/pattern/key/world_root and never the label, and `scope::extent_covers` only enlarges its haystack).

observe.rs 260-540: `printed.push_str(&stdout)` and the per-file `by_file` map are both built from the same `stdout` and are independent allocations; the Search label is formatted after the push, so the stated one-directional dataflow is what the code shape permits. The mint half (label copied verbatim into the extent, pin hashing label+world_root+world_state+output) is F4 in this workspace; the exclusion_note "listed rather than counted" ground is F5.

records.prop: The `Search` observation's label is the only part of a grep census that reaches a committed memo — the Facts table's Extent column is the labels joined and nothing else, and captured output is deliberately never rendered — so recording the bound anywhere but the label leaves a reader of the memo unable to see that the author's return was cut.
verdicts: True for the reader of a committed memo, and the memo spends it on a second audience it does not cover. C3 establishes that the label is NECESSARY — nothing else reaches the Facts table. The prose converts that to sufficiency ("it is the only place that works") and the design annotates only the label. But per F3, `look` hands the author `outcome.printed` and nothing else on both surfaces (main.rs 506-509, mcp.rs 643-645); the label first reaches the author in the `fact` result's `folded` array (mcp.rs 663-676), by which time the note asserting over that search has already been supplied as an input parameter. So under the design as written the author who reads a bounded return sees no indication it was bounded at the moment they read it, and learns of the cut only after committing the assertion. The condition C3 holds under is "reader" meaning a later reader of the memo; it establishes nothing about the author, who is the party the ticket's defect ("truncation breaks the coupling between 'looked' and 'saw'") is about.

The supporting mechanics are all confirmed — compose.rs's Extent cell is `f.extent.iter().map(|e| e.label.as_str()).join("; ")`, keys are deliberately not rendered, and "Captured output is not rendered either" is in the function's own doc comment — and the second half (look returns `printed` alone on both front ends, so the label is not a surface the author has read at capture time) is confirmed independently. The clause that overreaches is "the `Search` observation's label is the only part of a grep census that reaches a committed memo". The join takes *every* extent entry's label, so each per-file `GrepMatch` label (`{file} (grep: {pattern})`) reaches the memo too. What is true is that *labels* are the only part of a census that reaches it; the Search label is the right home for a whole-search bound because the bound is a property of the search, not of any one file — which is a different argument from "the only part".

compose.rs `render_facts` builds the Extent cell as every extent entry's label joined with "; " and its doc says only the label is rendered and captured output is not rendered at all. Per-file GrepMatch labels are `{file} (grep: {pattern})` with no measure of the return, and the per-file entries are built from the full stdout (F2). `look` returning `printed` alone on both front ends is F5 (main.rs:508, mcp.rs:644).

grep is invoked with -H and -n unconditionally, so every stdout line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>`, and `for line in stdout.lines() { line.split_once(':') }` is exactly how the per-file GrepMatch records are built. A cut at an arbitrary byte offset would hand back a partial final line, which is not a match record.

The reason given is sound — a mid-line cut does hand the author a fragment that is not a match record — but the rule the design derives from it ("accumulate whole lines, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget") has no floor, and with C8's 32768 it admits a return of zero content whenever the first candidate line exceeds the budget. That state is reachable here, not hypothetical: F1(7) finds four tracked files in this worktree with a single line over 32768 bytes (up to 905745), and F1(4) confirms `look_path` filters nothing, so any of them can be opened directly. The claim as written establishes only that the cut must fall on a line boundary; it does not establish that a line-boundary cut always returns something, and the design nowhere states what happens when it returns nothing. Either state the floor (admit at least one line, cutting it mid-line and saying so) or state explicitly that a line longer than the budget is unreturnable — the current wording leaves an implementer to discover the zero-byte case in production.

Everything measurable here checks out: grep is run with -I -n -H so its output line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>` and `look_grep` splits on `stdout.lines()`; exactly four tracked paths hold a single line over 32768 bytes, up to 905745, and all four are *.tetel/facts.jsonl snapshot ledgers (F3); a whole-`src` grep for `is_char_boundary`, `char_indices` and `.truncate(` returns no hits at all (F3); the longest single line carries 1922 UTF-8 continuation bytes (F6). The clause that does not hold as written is "`look_path` refuses only a missing path and a directory": `look_path` has a third refusal in its body, `invalid --lines range {a}:{b}` when `a < 1 || a > b` (observe.rs:300-302). The conclusion the clause is used for is unaffected — no exclusion filtering is applied and a plain `look <path>` with no range reaches none of the three refusals, so each of the four ledgers is readable directly — but the enumeration is incomplete.

The conclusion survives; the inference stated for it does not. C5 argues: the whole-lines-only rule "admits a return of no content at all whenever the first candidate line by itself exceeds the budget, and that state is reachable on tracked files here rather than hypothetical: exactly four tracked paths in this worktree hold a single line longer than 32768 bytes … while `look_path` refuses only a missing path and a directory and applies no exclusion filtering, so each is readable directly".

Holding a long line somewhere is not the same as the FIRST candidate line being over budget, and the claim's evidence establishes only the former. Measured (F1): in all four files the long line sits at position 11/15, 15, 2 and 2 — never position 1 — with first lines of 978, 882, 1273 and 1237 bytes. Reading each of them "directly", i.e. a plain `look <path>`, returns 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines (24948, 11977, 1274, 1238 bytes) and never zero content.

The condition C5 does not state, and needs: the zero-content state arises on a read whose selection BEGINS with the over-budget line — a ranged `look --lines k:…` with the long line at k (`--lines 15:20` on tet46, `--lines 2:2` on tet29). Under that condition the state is real and the floor is earned. As written, the claim's premise ("four tracked paths hold a long line") does not entail its conclusion ("that state is reachable" via the direct read it names), and the reader is left believing the plain read is the witness when it is not.

The rest of C5 — the line-boundary release rule, the character-boundary snap, the absence of any byte-safe cut in `src/`, the 1922 continuation bytes — is untouched by this.

Every measured component of C5 is exact — F3 reproduces all of them independently: exactly four tracked paths hold a line over 32768 bytes and all four are tetel's own .tetel/facts.jsonl ledgers, largest line 905745; the over-budget positions are 11 and 15 of 20, 15 of 21, 2 of 11, 2 of 10; a selection from line 1 releases 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines and never floors; the longest output line across the nine censuses is 1090 bytes; a whole-src grep for is_char_boundary/char_indices/.truncate( returns no matches; the longest single line carries 1922 UTF-8 continuation bytes. The grep line shape and the split unit are as stated.

records.prop: The bound cannot be derived from the caller's cap: the MCP `look` handler receives no field carrying one and returns `printed` unmeasured, so any number tetel applies is chosen by a person. Following this crate's own handling of an arbitrary number — `describe_buffer`, which refuses to invent a staleness threshold on the grounds that "a number chosen here would be arbitrary" and reports instead — the constant must be documented as a judgement and the design's load must rest on the report, not on the number.

records.prop: Nothing in this crate's source truncates anything today — a whole-`src` grep for `truncat` finds only one doc comment, about acknowledgements being untruncatable — so f3 introduces a new behaviour rather than moving an existing one, and there is no in-crate convention for how a truncation should be spelled.
verdicts: Counterexample on the axis the evidence never searched. `transplants::refuse_incomplete` (transplants.rs 428-440) truncates a premise's text to its first line before showing it to the author and marks the cut with a trailing ` …`. That is a truncation in this crate's source today, released at a line boundary, in text the author reads — so both halves of C7 fail: it is not true that "nothing in this crate's source truncates anything today", and it is not true that "there is no in-crate convention for how a truncation should be spelled". F8's grep for the word `truncat` could not have found it, because the code never uses that word; the claim rests on a name search standing in for a behaviour search. The design consequence is small but real: an in-crate spelling exists and f3's label segment departs from it (it reports how much was withheld, which the transplant elision does not), and the memo asserts there was nothing to depart from, so the departure is never argued.

The citation is exact — transplants.rs:432-435 is the loop that takes `text.lines().next()`, appends ` …` only under `text.lines().count() > 1`, and pushes the result. Cut on a line boundary: yes. Marker only when lines were dropped: yes (a single-line premise gets `first.to_string()` with no marker). No count of what was dropped anywhere in `shown` or `msg`: confirmed. The whole-src grep for `truncat` returning only a doc comment is also confirmed at this HEAD.
Confirms the second half: the single `truncat` hit in src is acks.rs:25, a `//!` doc comment about the ack log being monotone, not a truncation implementation.

records.prop: This design recommends 32768 bytes (32 KiB) as the bound, declared in the source as a judgement and not as a measurement. Its only stated constraint is that it be strictly below whatever cap the caller applies, and since tetel cannot observe that cap the value is chosen conservatively; its consequence on the nine censuses measured here is that seven of them (claim, fact, check, prose, ack, render, get) return bounded and two (target at 24974 bytes, label at 8201) return whole.
verdicts: The consequence is reproduced with margin. Rebuilding look_grep's exact grep invocation, the seven censuses claim/fact/check/prose/ack/render/get come to 162183/124840/123826/81081/74680/61431/44497 bytes of stdout alone, every one far above 32768; target and label come to 24261 and 7488 bytes of stdout, and to 24975 and 8202 as full returns (stdout plus the `({note})\n` exclusion line, whose byte-exact reconstruction is 714 with the six-memo list that predates this memo's own .md). The stated 24974 and 8201 are exactly those returns less the trailing newline, so both figures are reproducible under a stated convention. Worth knowing, not a defect: these two numbers embed the exclusion note, which lists rendered memo paths, so they drift as memos are added — the seven-bounded/two-whole conclusion does not.

records.prop: The plain `look <path>` and `look --lines A:B` paths must be left alone by this design, because in `look_path` the returned bytes and the captured `output` are the same value `shown`; bounding the return there would necessarily change what is captured, which the ticket puts out of scope. `look_grep` is bounded and `look_path` is not, and that asymmetry is a consequence of the code's shape, not an oversight.
verdicts: The claim's premise is right and its inference is false. In `look_path` (observe.rs 268-336) `printed` is a separate String assembled by `printed.push_str(&shown)` at line 316 — a byte copy — and `shown` is moved into `PendingEntry.output` afterwards at line 325. Two independent Strings exist between those points, which is the same separation `look_grep` exploits. Bounding `printed` after line 316 would therefore NOT "necessarily change what is captured": the capture would be byte-identical, exactly as C2 says it is on the grep path. So the asymmetry is not "a consequence of the code's shape"; it is a choice the design is entitled to make but has not justified. This matters because C9 is an instruction to an implementer — it tells them the `look <path>` case is closed by construction, which suppresses the observation that after f3 ships, `look <path>` on a large file is still silently cut by the caller with no trace anywhere, the very defect the ticket names.

The cited range is exact: observe.rs:314-330 is `let mut printed = String::new();` … `printed.push_str(&shown);` … then `PendingEntry { … output: shown, … }`. `shown` is copied into `printed` by borrow and only moved into the entry afterwards, so the two strings are independent and a bound on `printed` cannot reach the captured output, label or key.

records.prop: `look --lines` already contains this design's pattern in miniature: when the requested range runs past the end of the file the label records what was actually delivered rather than what was asked (`lines {a}-{end}` with `end = b.min(total)`, or an explicit "nothing in range" for an empty result), so recording a shortfall in the observation label is an established convention in this module rather than a new invention.
verdicts: observe.rs:296-313 is verbatim what the claim quotes: `let end = b.min(total);` with label `{path} lines {a}-{end}`, and the a>total branch labelling `{path} lines {a}-{b} (file has {total} line(s); nothing in range)`. The label therefore states the delivered range, not the requested one, so annotating a shortfall in the observation label already exists in this module.

The label therefore states the delivered range, not the requested one, so annotating a shortfall in the observation label already exists in this module.

records.prop: `look_grep` is the only function this design changes, and the change is contained: a whole-worktree census finds it in two files — the definition at src/observe.rs:349 and the one call site in `dispatch` at observe.rs:506, the remaining three occurrences being doc comments. Because the bound and the label are both assembled inside the function and its signature is unchanged, no caller has to be touched.
verdicts: Every number checks out on this HEAD: look_grep occurs five times across src/observe.rs and src/worldstate.rs — definition at observe.rs:349, the single dispatch call at observe.rs:506, doc mentions at observe.rs:76, observe.rs:495 and worldstate.rs:76; look_path four times in src/observe.rs alone — definition 277, dispatch call 516, doc mentions 4 and 495. No test file, no binary and no other module names either. One point of care rather than a qualification: a raw whole-worktree grep also matches rendered memos, `.evidence.jsonl` files and `.tetel/` ledgers, which is exactly the tetel-output class a census withholds, so "five times in two files" is the census's count, not the raw grep's.

records.prop: A bounded return changes nothing about what TET-28's census refusal guarantees, and its refusal text needs no change. The refusal fires on `ExtentEntry::censuses`, which reads the search's existence and its root out of an immutable extent that a bound applied to `printed` does not touch; and the text already disclaims the reading a bounded return would threaten, saying the refusal "is about the search's existence and where it was rooted, never about what it found".
verdicts: `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads only kind, pattern, world_root and key from the extent — never the returned text — and the target refusal fires on `fact.extent.iter().any(|e| e.censuses(symbol))`, so a bound on `printed` cannot change whether it fires. The refusal text at targets.rs:171 already ends "The refusal is about the search's existence and where it was rooted, never about what it found", which is exactly the disclaimer a bounded return would otherwise need added.

records.prop: Hitting the bound must not be an error at the destination: `look_grep` returns the bounded text as a successful `LookOutcome` exactly as it returns a whole one, and records the shortfall in the label rather than refusing. This follows the crate's own report-rather-than-refuse handling of an arbitrary number in `describe_buffer`, and it is forced anyway — the pending entries are already written from the full stdout by the time any bound is applied, so a refusal would have to discard a capture that already happened.
verdicts: The first two sentences hold: look_grep's only success path is `Ok(LookOutcome { printed })`, there is no error return keyed to result size, and the label is the natural place for the shortfall. The final clause — "it is forced anyway — the pending entries are already written from the full stdout by the time any bound is applied, so a refusal would have to discard a capture that already happened" — is not what observe.rs:415-479 shows. On the match branch `printed.push_str(&stdout)` runs *first*, before `by_file` is built and before any PendingEntry is constructed; and `pending::save(workspace_dir, &buf)?` is the last statement before the `Ok`. So an implementation bounding while assembling `printed` (which is how C2 describes it) reaches the bound before the entries exist and before anything is persisted, and could return `Err` without discarding any capture. Report-rather-than-refuse is a good choice here, but it is a choice, not something the code's ordering forces.

I read every `workspace::refuse` site the crate-wide sweep found (F3 for the sweep, F7 for the texts): all are missing/malformed input, a nonexistent or withdrawn referent, a forbidden flag combination, or a provenance/precondition failure with a singular remedy. None is conditioned on a measurement of a result. The ordering claim (`printed.push_str(&stdout)` before `by_file` and before any PendingEntry; `pending::save` the last statement before `Ok`) is F2; the targets.rs discriminator text and the census refusal wording are F5; describe_buffer's "a number chosen here would be arbitrary" is F4.

records.prop: The bound cannot disturb observation identity at the destination: the `Search` entry is keyed by `search_key(root_path, &m.root)` and each per-file entry by `resolve_key(Path::new(&file))`, both computed from paths alone, so two searches of the same root for the same pattern overlap each other whether either was bounded or not.
verdicts: Both key functions take only paths: resolve_key is fs::canonicalize with a path fallback, search_key resolves the root and picks between that spelling and the world root by canonical equality. Neither reads the pattern or any part of stdout, and the call sites in look_grep are exactly search_key(root_path, &m.root) for the Search entry and resolve_key(Path::new(&file)) per matched file, so a bound on printed cannot move a key.

records.prop: The bound earns its own `NON_COVERAGE` line rather than being folded into an existing one. The list already discriminates a withholding tetel chose (the tetel-output exclusion) from platform accidents that "contemplate nothing tetel chose" (grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files); a bound tetel applies to its own return is of the first kind. What the line states is a gap `check` genuinely cannot close: a fact's extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it — `scope.rs` names that limit as permanently out of reach and does not claim otherwise.
verdicts: The NON_COVERAGE list does make the discrimination the claim relies on, in the source comment's own words: the symlink/binary entry "names two *platform accidents* and contemplates nothing tetel chose", and the tetel-output exclusion is kept as "A separate line, deliberately not folded into the one above… A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here." A bound tetel applies to its own return is a deliberate withholding, so by that stated standard it earns its own line.

The second half holds too: nothing in the tool establishes that an author examined what an extent records, and scope.rs's module doc registers exactly that as out of reach — "Whether the note is *correct* about the location it names is exactly the limit this project registered as permanently out of reach ('insincere examination' — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation). Nothing here touches that." It states the limit rather than claiming coverage of it.

This claim instructs an implementer what a declared modification target (`NON_COVERAGE`) must say, and what it specifies is census-shaped while the design is not. Its content sentence is "a fact's extent records the whole search, and nothing anywhere establishes that the author read all of it", and the prose spends it the same way ("the list carries the general statement that a census's return to its author is bounded"), as does C16 ("the static list says a census reports the tree minus what tetel withheld"). But C9 and C20 put `look_path` inside the same bound, and F1(4) confirms a plain `look <path>` is a wholly different act — no search, no root, no exclusions, an extent naming one file and a range. An implementer who writes the line this claim specifies leaves every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in `check`'s non-coverage list, which is the one surface the design nominates for the general case. The single-line decision may well still be right, but the line has to be written for both acts — "what `look` returns to its author is bounded, and nothing establishes the author read the whole of what the extent records" — not for a census. As it stands the claim's own wording, followed literally, produces a line that covers `look_grep` only.

report.rs:86-190 carries both entries and the comment between them verbatim: the platform-accident entry ("symlinked directories and binary files"), the tetel-output entry, and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here". No entry in the list concerns what `look` returned to its author. `look_path` applying no exclusion filtering is F2 and is also stated in the tetel-output entry itself; scope.rs naming interpretation/insincere examination as permanently out of reach is F5.

The claim's own generalising argument does not stop where the claim stops it, and the standing line it specifies will mislead by contrast.

C15 argues correctly that a `NON_COVERAGE` line phrased about a search "would leave every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in the list, which is the one surface this design nominates for the general case", and concludes the line must say: "what `look` returned to its author is bounded, and a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it."

Run that argument one step further. `look` is not the only verb that writes an observation into the pending buffer and hands its author a return the caller then cuts. `run` does the same: `run_command` captures the child's merged stdout/stderr, pushes a `Proc` PendingEntry whose `output` is that capture, and returns it whole and unmeasured; both front ends hand it straight back with no size check — `print!("{}", outcome.printed)` at src/main.rs:526 and `"output": outcome.printed` at src/mcp.rs:653-656 (F3). The `run` tool's own description at src/mcp.rs:649 documents the large case explicitly ("a command whose output is enormous … puts that in a repository forever"). So a `run` observation has precisely the defect this design exists to remove — the coupling between what was captured and what the author saw is broken by the caller, silently — and after f3 it is not merely unfixed but affirmatively contrasted against, because the new standing line names `look`.

The condition C15 does not state: its second half — "a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it" — is true of every fact in the ledger regardless of which verb captured it, but the line as specified scopes it to `look`. A reader of `check`'s standing non-coverage will reasonably infer the caveat does not apply to `run`-captured facts, which is exactly backwards: those are the ones with no bound, no shortfall segment and no trace at all.

Not a demand that f3 bound `run` — that is a scoping decision the design may keep. What is owed is either a line whose general half is not verb-scoped, or a stated reason why `run` is excluded from a statement the design itself calls the general case.

The verifiable parts hold. The standing list does discriminate a chosen withholding from platform accidents, and its comment says verbatim "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here", beside the entry naming grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files. The first half's factual load is correct: `run_command` returns the child's whole captured output unmeasured with no length test anywhere in the function, and both front ends hand it back whole (`print!("{}", outcome.printed)` in main.rs's Run arm; `"output": outcome.printed` in the MCP run tool); the run tool's own description does contemplate "a command whose output is enormous" and answers by warning rather than bounding. `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering at all.

The qualification is the clause "`scope.rs` names that second half as permanently out of reach". The only occurrence of "permanently out of reach" in the whole of src/ is src/scope.rs:42, and what it registers there is a different proposition: "Whether the note is *correct* about the location it names is exactly the limit this project registered as permanently out of reach (\"insincere examination\" — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation)." That is about the truth of an author's interpretation of a location, not about how much of a capture the author was shown. Reading it as naming the second half ("a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it") requires stretching "insincere examination" from not-examined to not-shown, and scope.rs does not spell that out. This matters because it is the clause carrying the memo's assurance that the new entry "names an old limit that had been invisible rather than admitting a new weakness" — after the bound, `look` genuinely shows the author less than the extent records, which is new. Separate, non-blocking: the list itself is `NON_COVERAGE` in src/report.rs:86, not in scope.rs; C15 does not misattribute it, but the two files are easy to conflate here.

report.rs:86-190 carries both entries and the comment between them verbatim: the platform-accident entry ("symlinked directories and binary files"), the tetel-output entry, and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here". No entry in the list concerns what `look` returned to its author. `look_path` applying no exclusion filtering is F2 and is also stated in the tetel-output entry itself; scope.rs naming interpretation/insincere examination as permanently out of reach is F5.

The claim's own generalising argument does not stop where the claim stops it, and the standing line it specifies will mislead by contrast.

C15 argues correctly that a `NON_COVERAGE` line phrased about a search "would leave every bounded path read with no standing statement anywhere in the list, which is the one surface this design nominates for the general case", and concludes the line must say: "what `look` returned to its author is bounded, and a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it."

Run that argument one step further. `look` is not the only verb that writes an observation into the pending buffer and hands its author a return the caller then cuts. `run` does the same: `run_command` captures the child's merged stdout/stderr, pushes a `Proc` PendingEntry whose `output` is that capture, and returns it whole and unmeasured; both front ends hand it straight back with no size check — `print!("{}", outcome.printed)` at src/main.rs:526 and `"output": outcome.printed` at src/mcp.rs:653-656 (F3). The `run` tool's own description at src/mcp.rs:649 documents the large case explicitly ("a command whose output is enormous … puts that in a repository forever"). So a `run` observation has precisely the defect this design exists to remove — the coupling between what was captured and what the author saw is broken by the caller, silently — and after f3 it is not merely unfixed but affirmatively contrasted against, because the new standing line names `look`.

The condition C15 does not state: its second half — "a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed while nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it" — is true of every fact in the ledger regardless of which verb captured it, but the line as specified scopes it to `look`. A reader of `check`'s standing non-coverage will reasonably infer the caveat does not apply to `run`-captured facts, which is exactly backwards: those are the ones with no bound, no shortfall segment and no trace at all.

Not a demand that f3 bound `run` — that is a scoping decision the design may keep. What is owed is either a line whose general half is not verb-scoped, or a stated reason why `run` is excluded from a statement the design itself calls the general case.

The verifiable parts hold. The standing list does discriminate a chosen withholding from platform accidents, and its comment says verbatim "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here", beside the entry naming grep skipping symlinked directories and binary files. The first half's factual load is correct: `run_command` returns the child's whole captured output unmeasured with no length test anywhere in the function, and both front ends hand it back whole (`print!("{}", outcome.printed)` in main.rs's Run arm; `"output": outcome.printed` in the MCP run tool); the run tool's own description does contemplate "a command whose output is enormous" and answers by warning rather than bounding. `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering at all.

The qualification is the clause "`scope.rs` names that second half as permanently out of reach". The only occurrence of "permanently out of reach" in the whole of src/ is src/scope.rs:42, and what it registers there is a different proposition: "Whether the note is *correct* about the location it names is exactly the limit this project registered as permanently out of reach (\"insincere examination\" — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation)." That is about the truth of an author's interpretation of a location, not about how much of a capture the author was shown. Reading it as naming the second half ("a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it") requires stretching "insincere examination" from not-examined to not-shown, and scope.rs does not spell that out. This matters because it is the clause carrying the memo's assurance that the new entry "names an old limit that had been invisible rather than admitting a new weakness" — after the bound, `look` genuinely shows the author less than the extent records, which is new. Separate, non-blocking: the list itself is `NON_COVERAGE` in src/report.rs:86, not in scope.rs; C15 does not misattribute it, but the two files are easy to conflate here.
