records.prop: There is no act that gets an author the rest of a bounded census, and this design does not add one. Narrowing the root or the pattern is not available as a remedy, because a census is "one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself" and a narrowed search stops qualifying as one; `look --grep` takes no other parameter that could page or filter. What remains available is an additional search rooted at a subdirectory, recorded as its own observation alongside the census rather than in place of it — and, outside the return path entirely, the per-file `GrepMatch` entries, which hold every matched line and ship complete into the snapshot.
verdicts: The escape hatch the claim points at is real: mint stores every non-empty pending output in full into the fact, and that facts.jsonl ships in the snapshot beside the memo, so the per-file GrepMatch entries — which hold every matched line — are recoverable there even when the return was cut. The census-narrowing half is settled by the target refusal's own words ("a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself") together with `censuses` requiring key == world_root, so a subdirectory-rooted search cannot qualify; and `look --grep` takes no paging or filtering parameter — LookParams is workspace/path/grep/lines, and lines is refused outright when combined with grep. Re-reading a bounded plain `look <path>` with `--lines A:B` keys on resolve_key(p) regardless of range, so it overlaps the first read.

The `look_path` half of this claim — "`--lines A:B` is already a first-class parameter of the same verb, so the author reads the rest of the file by asking for it" — is broken by a state reachable on tracked files in this worktree.

Construction. Take `look /Volumes/SSD/Documents/lonic/tetel/docs/design/tet46-look-never-returns-tetel-content.md.tetel/facts.jsonl`. F1(7) measures it: 20 lines, of which two exceed 32768 bytes, the longest 905745. F1(4) confirms `look_path` applies no exclusion filtering of any kind, so a named snapshot path is read like any other file — nothing stops this call. Under the rule the design states ("accumulate whole lines, and stop before the first line that would carry the total past the byte budget", C5/C20), the return stops at whichever over-budget line comes first. The author then asks for the rest with `--lines k:20`. The selection now BEGINS with a 905745-byte line, no whole line fits under 32768, and the bound admits zero lines: the author gets the `==> path <==` header, an empty body, and a label reading "showed 0 of N lines (32768-byte bound)". Every range that includes that line behaves identically. There is no `--lines` argument that returns any byte of it, so the claim's remedy does not reach it, and "needs nothing new either" is false: this case needs something the design does not have (a floor of one line, a byte-level fallback for an over-budget line, or at minimum an explicit statement that an over-budget line is unreadable through `look`).

Worse than the status quo on exactly the axis the ticket cares about. Today the caller truncates at ~59 KB, so the author reading that file sees its first ~59 KB. Under the design they see zero bytes of that line. The memo's answer to "what does an author do" is that the design "does not give the author back what was withheld; it stops the withholding from being secret" — but here the design withholds strictly more than the status quo did, and this claim asserts a remedy that does not exist.

The same construction reaches `look_grep`: a grep whose matching line is one of these long JSON lines emits a `<file>:<lineno>:<text>` line over the budget, and if it is the first matching line the bounded return is empty while the label still says "N files matched". The prose's consolation that "even a heavily bounded return still tells the author truthfully how many files matched" is then a file count attached to nothing.

The CLI `Look` command has exactly `path`, `--lines A:B` and `--grep PATTERN` — no paging, offset, limit or filtering parameter — and the MCP handler takes the same three plus `workspace` (F5). The census definition "a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself" is verbatim at targets.rs:168 (F5). GrepMatch entries holding every matched line, and the `Path` entry's output being the complete selected text with the key resolved before any range handling, are F2; facts.jsonl shipping as the first SNAPSHOT_FILES entry is F4.

C18's universal about the residue is false as written, and the true version is a worse residue than the one stated. The claim says: "What `--lines` does not reach is a single line longer than the budget: on such a line every range containing it returns the same floor — its first bytes up to a character boundary at or below 32768 — and no argument to `look` returns the remainder."

Constructed counterexample from the measured line lengths (F1). Take tet46 …/facts.jsonl: 20 lines, with 905745 bytes at line 15 and lines 12/13/14 at 4585/4320/2945 bytes. Ask `--lines 12:20`. That range contains line 15. Under C5's release rule the selection accumulates lines 12, 13 and 14 (11853 bytes with newlines), then stops before line 15 because it would carry the total past 32768. A whole line fitted, so the floor does not fire. The return contains zero bytes of line 15 and is not "the same floor".

The condition C18 does not state: the floor is returned only by a range that BEGINS at the over-budget line. Every other range containing it returns none of it. So the author's recovery act is not "ask for a range containing it" but "ask for a range starting exactly at it" — and to know which k that is, they must already know where the long line sits, which the bounded return does not tell them (the label reports N of M, not which line overran). The residue is therefore larger than C18 states: not merely "the remainder of that line is unreachable", but "the floored prefix itself is reachable only from one specific range start, discoverable only by bisection".

The claim's headline — that no act gets the author the rest of a bounded return, and that the escape hatch is the fact's captured `output` in the snapshot — is unaffected.

The measurements are exact. Simulating the release rule under 32768 bytes on the tet46 …/facts.jsonl ledger: `--lines 12:20` releases lines 12-14 at 11852 bytes and no byte of line 15; `--lines 8:20` releases three whole lines (8-10) and no byte of line 11. The census remedies are closed as stated: src/targets.rs carries verbatim "a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself", and `look --grep` takes no paging or filtering parameter — `LookParams` (src/mcp.rs:211-227) has exactly workspace/path/lines/grep, and the CLI reaches look_grep through `LookRequest::Grep { pattern, root }` with nothing further. The per-file GrepMatch entries hold every matched line and facts.jsonl is the first entry of SNAPSHOT_FILES.

The qualification is the clause "but never which line of the selection overran". On a floored return C20 fixes the label as `<path> lines {a}-{end} — showed 0 of M lines; first line cut mid-line at B of L bytes (32768-byte bound)`. "first line" names which line of the selection overran, and combined with the `lines {a}-{end}` segment it names the file line too (it is a). So the "never" is over-strong for exactly the case the same sentence has just described. The claim's substance survives: on a bounded but unfloored return — the case the bisection argument is about — the label reports only how many whole lines were shown and does not say the next one was over budget rather than merely not fitting, so the position is not recoverable from it and bisection is the honest description.

records.prop: The `prose-revised-since-proof` listing is a pure function of three recomputed quantities and stores none of them: a block's current (text, cite-list) pair, the timestamp at which that exact pair first appeared in the block's event history, and an anchor equal to the maximum over the block's cited claims of each claim's earliest non-refuting record whose proposition digest matches the claim's current wording. The block is listed exactly when the pair's first-appearance timestamp exceeds the anchor, and is skipped outright when it is a heading, when its current cite-list is empty, or when no cited claim has such a record.
verdicts: checks.rs:414-557 states each element: first_proof per claim = earliest non-Refutes record whose proposition_digest equals sha256 of the claim's current proposition; anchor = max of those over the block's cited claims; block_timestamp = min timestamp among versions whose (text, cite) both equal the current pair; push iff block_timestamp > anchor; `continue` on heading, on empty current cite-list, and on the existential gate (no cited claim in first_proof). All recomputed per call from prose_events/claims/evidence; nothing derived is persisted.

`prose_after_proof` takes exactly (prose_events, claims, evidence) and recomputes all three quantities in-body: the current (text, cite) pair from the replayed history, the min timestamp over versions whose text AND cite both equal the current pair, and `anchor = max` over cited claims of the earliest record whose `proposition_digest == sha256_hex(claim.proposition)` and whose verdict is not `Refutes`. Pushes iff `block_timestamp > anchor`; `continue`s on `h.heading`, on `cur_cite.is_empty()`, and on `cited.is_empty()` (the existential gate). Nothing is persisted.

records.prop: A sibling `acks.jsonl`, added to `snapshot::SNAPSHOT_FILES`, degrades safely in the older build it will be shipped past: that constant is an explicit enumeration whose stated purpose is that a future workspace file be a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, so a build that predates the entry simply never opens the file, reads `prose.jsonl` unchanged, and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing. The failure direction is therefore over-reporting a residue entry a newer build would suppress, never suppressing one an older build would show.
verdicts: C4's dominance sentence — "The failure direction is therefore over-reporting a residue entry a newer build would suppress, never suppressing one an older build would show" — is refuted by construction. It reasons only about the READ side (an old build never opens acks.jsonl). The WRITE side breaks it. `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) copies `SNAPSHOT_FILES` and never removes anything already in `<memo>.tetel/`, and skips any entry absent from the workspace. `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is a per-build constant. Construction: (1) author acks block P in workspace W with a new build and runs `render --out` — the snapshot now holds acks.jsonl = [Ack(P, key k)]; (2) author reconsiders and appends `Unack(P)`, so W's log is [Ack, Unack] and P must list again; (3) the memo is re-rendered by a build predating the SNAPSHOT_FILES entry — exactly "the older build it will be shipped past" that C4 posits. That build refreshes prose.jsonl, claims.jsonl and the memo bytes, and leaves the stale acks.jsonl in place because it does not know the name. (4) A newer build's `check` reads `snapshot_dir/acks.jsonl` (src/lib.rs:150-211 shows every residue input comes from the snapshot dir), finds [Ack] with key k still matching the recomputed text/cites/digests, and suppresses P — an entry both the older build and the true workspace state say should be shown. Nothing reddens: `compose::render` (src/compose.rs:79-95) reads only prose/claims/targets/transplants/facts, so acks.jsonl is outside the provenance-drift comparison by design (C13). The same state is reachable with a single build and no mixed builds at all, via the documented "A file absent from the workspace is skipped rather than erroring" path: render once from a workspace holding an ack, then re-render after that workspace's acks.jsonl is gone (restored/rebuilt workspace), and the stale ack keeps suppressing.

Nothing in snapshot.rs, compose.rs or lib.rs enumerates the snapshot directory (no fs::read_dir outside observe.rs/scope.rs/workspace.rs), and compose::render reads only the five named logs, so a build predating the entry never opens acks.jsonl and reads prose.jsonl unchanged. SNAPSHOT_FILES' doc comment states the enumerate-don't-copy-wholesale purpose in the words the claim gives it. The over-report-never-under-report direction follows.

Both halves check out at source. `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit nine-entry enumeration whose doc states verbatim that it is "Enumerated rather than copied wholesale so that a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold" — a build predating an `acks.jsonl` entry never names the file and so never opens it, while still copying and reading `prose.jsonl`. And `snapshot::write`'s loop is `if src.exists() { fs::copy(...) }` with no removal pass, so a snapshot does retain a file the workspace no longer has.

The second half — "The writer must reconcile — deleting a snapshot file absent from the workspace — for the snapshot to mean 'the workspace at last render' rather than 'the most recent copy any build made of each file'" — does not say what the reconciliation enumerates, and the two available answers differ exactly on the cross-build case the claim's first half is about. `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) has only one enumeration in it, `for name in SNAPSHOT_FILES`, over a per-build `const [&str; 9]`, and never reads the snapshot directory. Reconciling over that constant leaves a tenth file a newer build wrote entirely unvisited by an older build's render, so the snapshot means "the workspace at last render, for the files the rendering build's manifest names, plus whatever any other build left behind" — which is the equality the claim says the fix establishes, and it is not established for the file this design adds. Reconciling over the snapshot directory instead does establish it, at the price of an older build deleting snapshot content it does not understand — a cost this memo never weighs, and a direct tension with `SNAPSHOT_FILES`' stated purpose that shipping or withholding a file be a deliberate per-build decision. Note the same residual hazard is what C14 cites to kill the withdrawal verb, so the two claims are consistent only under the manifest reading — under which this sentence's stated purpose is not achieved.

SNAPSHOT_FILES is an explicit nine-entry enumeration whose doc comment states the purpose the claim quotes ("a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`"); `write` iterates only that array, copies only `if src.exists()`, and contains no removal — so it accretes, and a build predating an `acks.jsonl` entry never visits the file. Reconciling over the manifest would indeed never visit an unnamed file, for the same reason.

The check side reads the snapshot's `prose.jsonl` by explicit name and computes the residue from it plus ledger claims and evidence records; nothing else in the snapshot feeds the finding, so a build predating the entry reads prose.jsonl unchanged and reproduces TET-30's un-suppressed listing.

"this needs two things rather than one" and "The writer must reconcile" hold only under a condition the claim does not state and that C14 removes: that the workspace's `acks.jsonl` can shrink. It cannot. `append_jsonl` opens with `.append(true)`, no production verb in src/ deletes a workspace log (all 21 `fs::remove*` matches are `#[cfg(test)]` scratch cleanup), and this design ships NO withdrawal verb (C14). So the workspace's ack log is monotone, and `snapshot::write`'s copy-only loop (src/snapshot.rs 135-146) can only leave the snapshot holding an EARLIER state of that log — a subset. A subset suppresses fewer blocks, i.e. over-reports, which is precisely the direction C4 declares acceptable. The under-reporting case the second leg exists to close — "a snapshot retains a log the workspace no longer has" — was reachable when an `Unack` event existed (it could invalidate an ack that the snapshot's stale copy still carried); once `Unack` is gone, reaching it requires an out-of-band act the memo does not name, such as deleting or restoring a workspace directory or re-rendering the memo from a different workspace, both of which also desynchronise `prose.jsonl` and `identity.json` and so surface through drift and grounding-provenance. This matters because C4 is an instruction to an implementer to change a shared, load-bearing writer, and C4 itself states the price: "a build reconciling over the directory deletes a snapshot file it does not understand". That price is general and permanent — every future snapshot file, including the TET-36 obligation ledger C19 plans to re-home these events into, becomes destroyable by any render from a build predating it, where today it would survive. The design pays a general, forward-facing destructive cost for a case its own no-withdrawal decision made unreachable through the tool. Either state the residual case reconciliation actually closes (and why it is worth that price), or narrow C4 to the manifest leg alone and drop `snapshot::write` from the modification targets.

Both load-bearing properties hold, but one supporting clause is false as written. Holds: SNAPSHOT_FILES (src/snapshot.rs:71) is an explicit `[&str; 9]` enumeration whose doc gives exactly the stated purpose ("a future workspace file is a deliberate decision to ship or withhold, not an accident of `cp -r`"), and `write` (snapshot.rs:135-146) only iterates it, so a build predating a tenth entry never opens the file and `write`'s body needs no change; `append_jsonl` (workspace.rs:451-456) is `create(true).append(true)` + `writeln!`, never truncating; no production code path deletes or truncates a workspace log. False as written: "none of it in the modules holding the authoring verbs" — the `fs::remove` sites are in review.rs, evidence.rs, facts.rs (559/576/589/599/601), workspace.rs and observe.rs, and facts.rs, observe.rs and workspace.rs are precisely the modules holding `fact`, `look`/`run` and `append_jsonl`. The removes are inside those modules' `#[cfg(test)]` regions, not absent from them, so the clause should say "in no production code path" rather than "in none of those modules". Secondarily, facts.rs:599 `remove_file(dir.join("refusals.log"))` is test *setup* (staging `a_snapshot_with_no_refusal_log_yields_no_windows`), not "scratch-directory teardown". Neither correction touches the monotonicity conclusion.

C4's conclusion "a snapshot's ack log, however stale, is a prefix of the workspace's: it holds a subset of the acks, suppresses a subset of the blocks, and therefore over-reports rather than under-reports" is refuted by construction on the workspace-identity axis, which neither of the claim's two premises addresses. The premises are about the ack log inside one workspace; the conclusion is about the snapshot's copy versus the workspace's, and the inference needs an unstated premise that a memo is only ever rendered from one workspace.

F2 witnesses that it is not: `render --out` (src/main.rs:826-858) takes its workspace from the free `--workspace` flag with nothing binding a memo path to a prior renderer, and `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) copies `for name in SNAPSHOT_FILES` under `if src.exists()` with no removal pass and no refusal, while re-minting and overwriting identity.json from whatever workspace it is handed. So: ack P in W1, `render --out M` (snapshot holds acks.jsonl=[Ack(P,k)]); later `--workspace W2 render --out M` where W2 has no acks.jsonl — a rebuilt state directory, a second machine, or a workspace reconstructed from the committed snapshot. The absent file is skipped rather than removed, the stale ack survives beside W2's prose and claims, and if P's text, cites and claim digests still match, P is suppressed with no acknowledgement anywhere in the rendering workspace. The snapshot's log is then a superset, not a prefix, and the direction is silent under-reporting. Nothing reddens: acks.jsonl is outside compose::render's inputs by C13's own choice, so drift cannot see it, and the log is well-formed so C11's unreadable disjunct does not fire.

This is one build, no mixed builds, no clock skew and no code path removing anything, so the revised premises do not close it. The withdrawn reconciliation pass was the only mechanism in the design that would have. Either restore a reconciliation (or a binding between a snapshot and the workspace identity that wrote it), or narrow C4 to the single-workspace case and propagate that narrowing into C16's cost argument and the "What changes, and what it costs" paragraph, which spend the unnarrowed one-directional guarantee.

Manifest, monotonicity and the identity gap all check out at the pin: SNAPSHOT_FILES is a nine-entry explicit enumeration whose doc comment states the ship-or-withhold purpose verbatim; snapshot::write copies present files and skips absent ones with no removal or reconciliation; --workspace is a free global clap flag with default_value "default" and the Render arm derives workspace_dir from it alone, never comparing against an existing <path>.tetel/. So a second workspace's render does leave a first workspace's acks.jsonl in place beside the second's prose/claims, while identity.json is overwritten — which is exactly the asymmetry the third (identity-equality) property closes.

records.prop: For a claims-unaffected prose edit — a typo or wording fix that leaves every cited claim's proposition untouched — both of TET-30's two clearing acts misrepresent what the author did. Restoring the text and citation list, which C6 names as the first act, restores the defect the edit corrected. Revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, C6's second act, requires changing a claim that is correct; and because `out_of_proof` is one of the disjuncts of `Findings::machine_check_failed` while `prose_revised_since_proof` is not, that route drives the run to a machine failure until a further grounding pass lands, spending a red check and a pass to silence a line that never failed the run.
verdicts: The substance holds at this pin: prose_after_proof's doc comment names exactly two clearing acts — "restoring the exact text and citations the claims settled under, or revising/adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded" — and checks.rs:216-229 lists `out_of_proof` among `machine_check_failed`'s disjuncts while `prose_revised_since_proof` is not among them, so the second act does redden the run until a further pass grades the new wording. The clause I cannot grade as written is the reference: the proposition attributes the naming of the two acts to "C6", and this memo's own C6 (per the brief) is about an acknowledged block still printing rather than vanishing — it names no clearing act. The reference reads correctly only as TET-30's C6, which C10 spells out and C5 does not.

The substance holds for the revise route: `prose_after_proof`'s doc names exactly the two clearing acts, restoring the exact prior text+citations does restore the corrected wording, `out_of_proof` IS a disjunct of `machine_check_failed` and `prose_revised_since_proof` is NOT, and `out_of_proof`'s own doc says the only remedy is to reprove. The failing clause is the disjunction "Revising **or adding** a cited claim". For the *adding* branch neither consequent holds: adding a new claim does not "require changing a claim that is correct", and a newly minted, ungrounded claim lands in `Findings::ungrounded_claims`, documented "Human-owed — absence of evidence is not itself a failure" and absent from `machine_check_failed`'s disjuncts — so that branch does not drive the run to a machine failure at all. The claim is true of revision and false of addition, and it asserts both.

Second record for the same qualification, grounding the part of it that lives outside F4's extent: `Findings::ungrounded_claims` is documented "Human-owed — absence of evidence is not itself a failure", so the "or adding a cited claim" branch of C5 does not redden the run via `out_of_proof` or any other disjunct of `machine_check_failed`.

`Findings::machine_check_failed` ORs out_of_proof among its disjuncts and does not mention prose_revised_since_proof, whose own field doc says "Human-owed, never a failure"; `out_of_proof` is documented as "every record on file grades a wording this claim no longer carries" — exactly the state a revision of a correct claim creates until a further pass lands.

TET-30's C6 names "Reverting the text and citations to what they were when the claims settled" first of the two clearing acts, and the ungrounded-claim branch reddens nothing: check 4 (unsettled citation) runs only against fenced tetel rows, never against ledger claims, so citing a newly minted ungrounded claim leaves machine_check_failed untouched.

Deleting the entry would make "no post-proof prose revision exists in this memo" and "one exists and a human has read it against its claims" indistinguishable in the check report, whereas this crate treats distinguishable states as owed distinct output — its no-rows path says so in as many words, that being "a distinct state from a clean run, not a weaker way of spelling it". Printing also costs nothing the residue does not already pay: the entry format already carries an author's own `--why` verbatim under `revised because:`, with the source comment stating that it is never a paraphrase and is the most actionable thing the entry can hand a reader.

records.prop: An acknowledged block should leave the `prose-revised-since-proof` group and be printed instead under one collapsed document-level bullet carrying, per acknowledged block, its id, its document line, its acknowledgement timestamp and the author's `--why` verbatim. This is the shape the crate already reaches for: the residue's own preamble is one document-level bullet, and the comment justifying it names `ledger_has_no_scope_columns` as precedent on the ground that a constant repeated per row buries the findings that are about this document. Leaving the block inside the demanding group with an extra annotation would keep a standing demand a human has already discharged, which is the skim-training failure the design exists to remove; removing it from the report entirely is refused by the preceding claim.

The load-bearing justification checks out: prose_after_proof's doc comment states that the ledger-derived proposition and claims.jsonl's are not the same string — compose::ledger_cell replaces embedded newlines with spaces and ledger::split_row_cells trims each cell — and that using claims.jsonl for the in-proof digest test would make such a claim drop out silently. Minting and re-checking the ack digest from claims.jsonl (which the snapshot ships) is therefore the source that makes an edge-whitespace or embedded-newline claim ackable, and the predicate as stated is pure equality over recomputed values with nothing derived stored. `workspace::now_unix()` is what stamps prose events, as the proposition says of every workspace event.

The load-bearing source claim — that the snapshot's `claims.jsonl` propositions and the ledger-derived ones are not the same string — is stated in `prose_after_proof`'s own doc comment: `compose::ledger_cell` "replaces embedded newlines with spaces" and `ledger::split_row_cells` "trims every cell", so a claim with an embedded newline or edge whitespace digests differently. `evidence::sha256_hex` and `workspace::now_unix()` both exist and every prose event already carries the latter (F3, F10). The predicate as described is pure equality over recomputed values, consistent with `prose_after_proof` storing nothing.

The load-bearing technical clause — that the ack's digests must come from the snapshot's claims.jsonl and deliberately not from the ledger-derived propositions the in-proof test uses — is established directly: compose.rs:314 `ledger_cell` does `.replace('\n', " ")`, ledger.rs:94 `split_row_cells` trims every cell, and checks.rs:365-375 states the converse requirement for prose_after_proof. So the two strings genuinely differ for a proposition with an embedded newline or edge whitespace, and digesting the ledger form would make such a claim unackable with nothing red to say so. Heading/empty-cite skipping and the pair key are as described in prose_after_proof.

The remaining components are expressible against existing API exactly as stated: workspace::now_unix() is the crate's event timestamp helper, and workspace::identity_of reads a snapshot directory's identity.json without minting one — which is what makes "records a workspace identity equal to the one in the snapshot's identity.json" a check that can be written rather than an aspiration.

records.prop: The sketch's second suppression clause — that the ack's timestamp be later than the recomputed anchor — is dropped, because it cannot fire. The rule is only consulted for a block the trigger already listed, and listing means the current pair's first-appearance timestamp already exceeds the anchor; an ack recording that same current pair is appended to an append-only log by the same authoring workspace, after that pair exists, and stamped by the same `workspace::now_unix()` that stamped the prose event. So unless the authoring machine's clock runs backwards between the two appends, the ack's timestamp exceeds the block timestamp which already exceeds the anchor, and the clause is satisfied in every case it is evaluated. Dropping it leaves the suppression predicate free of any timestamp comparison at all, which is why — unlike the trigger it guards — the acknowledgement does not rest on two clocks agreeing.
verdicts: Listing requires `block_timestamp > anchor` where block_timestamp is the *first* appearance of the current (text, cite) pair (checks.rs:539-553), so any event appended after that pair exists — including an ack recording it — carries a later stamp unless the clock moves backwards. `workspace::now_unix()` stamps prose events and would stamp the ack, and the logs are append-only. The dropped clause is therefore satisfied wherever it would be evaluated.

Listing is exactly `block_timestamp > anchor`, so the rule is only consulted for a block whose current pair's first-appearance timestamp already exceeds the anchor. `prose.jsonl` is append-only and both `create` and `revise` stamp `workspace::now_unix()` (F3), so an ack appended by the same workspace after that pair exists carries a timestamp >= the block timestamp under a non-retrograde clock. The dropped clause is therefore satisfied in every case it would be evaluated, and dropping it leaves the suppression predicate with no timestamp comparison.

records.prop: Three invalidation invariants follow from the key, each with the mutation that reddens its test. (i) Any later change to the block's text or to its citation list voids the ack, because both are components of the key; the mutation is to compare only the text, after which a citation-only revision — which TET-30's C6 records as an act that lists rather than clears — would stay suppressed. (ii) Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack, because the key carries that claim's proposition digest; the mutation is to drop the digest set from the key, after which an ack would outlive a rewrite of the very claim the author read the paragraph against. (iii) A workspace with no `acks.jsonl` produces byte-identical output to today's, because `workspace::read_jsonl` treats a missing file as an empty log rather than an error; the mutation is to make the missing file an error, after which every memo rendered before this design existed would fail to check.
verdicts: Invariant (iii) is stated over the wrong object. It says "A workspace with no `acks.jsonl` produces byte-identical output to today's, because `workspace::read_jsonl` treats a missing file as an empty log" — but the check never reads the workspace. src/lib.rs:150-211 takes every residue input from `snapshot_dir`, so the property that actually governs output is "a SNAPSHOT with no acks.jsonl", and the two are not equivalent: `snapshot::write` (src/snapshot.rs:135-146) never deletes a snapshot file and skips any workspace file that is absent, so a memo whose snapshot once received an acks.jsonl keeps it after the workspace's copy is gone. The invariant holds, as written, only for a memo whose snapshot has never received an ack log — which is the migration case it was presumably meant to cover, and should be the condition it states. Its proposed mutation-test ("make the missing file an error") also only exercises the never-acked case and would not catch the stale-snapshot case at all. The `read_jsonl`-treats-missing-as-empty half of the reasoning is correct; the quantifier over "a workspace" is what is wrong.

(iii) is exactly workspace::read_jsonl's NotFound arm returning `Ok(Vec::new())` (workspace.rs:461-465), and making that an error would fail every pre-existing memo.

C17 requires three new entries in `NON_COVERAGE`, and src/report.rs:486 prints `for item in NON_COVERAGE { ... "  - tetel does not catch: {item}" }` under no conditional at all, immediately above the build line, on every report the function produces. (ii) is a consequence of the key as C8 defines it.

records.prop: The acknowledgement is a strict filter over the trigger's output, applied after `prose_after_proof` has produced its list, and therefore cannot add a listing that TET-30 would not have produced — a stale, malformed or unmatched ack simply fails to suppress, which is the same state as no ack at all. Two consequences hold without further argument: the set of blocks the reader is asked to act on is always a subset of TET-30's, so no new false demand can be manufactured; and `machine_check_failed` is untouched, since `prose_revised_since_proof` is not among its disjuncts and the ack changes only which entries populate it. It also follows that the digest component does not close any part of TET-30's conceded non-coverage for prose that ships alongside a claim revision — it only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.
verdicts: `Findings::machine_check_failed` enumerates its disjuncts explicitly and `prose_revised_since_proof` is not one of them, so filtering the residue list cannot change the machine verdict. A filter applied after prose_after_proof has produced its list can only remove entries, so the acted-on set is a subset and an unmatched ack degrades to the no-ack state.

The conceded non-coverage the last sentence refers to is still standing verbatim in NON_COVERAGE: "false prose that ships alongside a claim revised in the same round — the ticket this check answers concedes it, and this design does not fix it". A suppression key is only consulted for a block already listed, so its digest component can close none of it.

The production call site is a single `let mut listed = checks::prose_after_proof(...)` whose result is then decorated and assigned to `findings.prose_revised_since_proof`, so a filter can only subtract from `listed`. `prose_revised_since_proof` is not among `machine_check_failed`'s disjuncts (F4), so the field's contents cannot change the machine verdict. The concession about prose shipping alongside a claim revision is already a standing `NON_COVERAGE` entry (F5), unaffected by a digest that only invalidates acks.

"a stale, malformed or unmatched ack simply fails to suppress, which is the same state as no ack at all" holds for stale and unmatched, but not for MALFORMED without an undeclared decision this memo does not make — and the decision it implies is one the codebase's own standard forbids here. `workspace::read_jsonl` (src/workspace.rs 458-472) does not degrade a bad line to an empty list: it maps any line's parse failure to `Err(InvalidData)` over the WHOLE log. So a malformed `acks.jsonl` yields Err, not "no acks". The only way to reach C11's stated behaviour is to read it under `if let Ok(...)` at the lib.rs call site, mirroring what that site already does for `prose.jsonl` — but lib.rs 172-211 justifies that silence with a premise specific to prose.jsonl, verbatim: the same file "already failed that earlier read too, and `findings.provenance` is already `Unreadable`, which `machine_check_failed` already reddens ... This `Err` arm is reachable only alongside a failure already reported elsewhere, never on its own". That premise is exactly what C13 and C21 remove for acks: because `compose::render` never reads `acks.jsonl`, `snapshot::check` never opens it, provenance is `Matches`, and the Err arm IS reachable on its own. The result is a check that reads an unparseable acknowledgement log, discards it, prints TET-30's listing, and says nothing anywhere about the log being unreadable — a green-except-for-the-residue run whose silence about a corrupt shipped record has no counterpart in this crate. The direction is safe (over-report, so C11's subset consequence survives), but the claim's "collapses to the same behaviour" conceals a fourth reporting decision the design owes: a malformed ack log must either redden, or earn a fourth NON_COVERAGE line beside C17's three.

Every source-anchored clause verified exactly. `workspace::read_jsonl` (workspace.rs:462-474) maps any line's parse failure into an `io::Error` returned for the whole log, never an empty one. The prose call site is `if let Ok(prose_events) = workspace::read_jsonl::<prose::ProseEvent>(...)` at lib.rs:198-201, and the comment at lib.rs:179-197 defends it on exactly the premise the claim names — the file was already read by `compose::render` -> `prose::load_all`, so provenance is already `Unreadable` and `machine_check_failed` already reddens it. `compose::render` (compose.rs:79-95) reads exactly prose, claims, targets, transplants and facts, so that premise is unavailable for a log render never reads. The quoted rule is byte-identical to checks.rs:230-233. `machine_check_failed` (checks.rs:216-228) has `out_of_proof` as a disjunct and not `prose_revised_since_proof`, and `prose_after_proof` (checks.rs:414-556) returns a single Vec of listed blocks, so a suppression rule can only be a filter over that output. The remaining clauses (that this is the design's only touch on `machine_check_failed`; that no ack moves a claim between partitions) are stipulations about code not yet written and are consistent with, but not stated by, the source.

records.prop: The minting surface is one verb, `tetel prose --ack <id> --why <text>` with the matching MCP argument pair, built as a variant of the single request shape both front ends already share so the two cannot drift on which missing flag is refused. Its refusals are exactly the workspace-decidable ones the existing prose verbs use, raised through the same `workspace::refuse` helper: no such block, the block is a heading, the block carries no citations, a cited id that does not resolve to a claim in `claims.jsonl`, and an empty `--why` — the last on the identical `why.trim().is_empty()` test that already backs "--revise requires --why (revisions must explain themselves)". None inspects the content or plausibility of the reason. The verb cannot refuse an ack on a block that is not currently listed, because an authoring workspace holds no evidence records at all — they live beside the rendered memo — so it cannot compute an anchor; and it need not, since an ack on an unlisted block suppresses nothing.
verdicts: "The minting surface is one verb" is true only of acknowledgement and false of the design, because C14 requires a second minting act — `Unack`, "carrying a block id and its own required verbatim `--why`" — and the memo's own implementation-surface paragraph says "the two verbs". C12 is the claim an implementer reads for what to build at the front end, and it is enumerative in both directions: one verb, and refusals that are "exactly the workspace-decidable ones ... and no others". Nothing in the ledger states the withdrawal verb's flag spelling, which of C12's five refusals apply to it (a block with no citations, or a heading, can never have been acked, so the ack refusals are not obviously the right set), whether an `Unack` on a block with no prior ack is refused or accepted as a no-op, or what its `ProseOutcome` is. F1 shows why that gap costs something concrete: each verb is a mode of one shared request shape, selected by an `if let Some(..) else if let Some(..)` chain duplicated in src/main.rs:773-810 and src/mcp.rs:735-744, and an unspecified second mode is exactly where the two front ends drift — which is the property C12 invokes the shared shape to guarantee. The claim should either say "two verbs" and enumerate the second's refusals, or narrow itself explicitly to the acknowledgement verb and let a sibling claim carry withdrawal.

The clause I cannot grade as written is "Its refusals are exactly the workspace-decidable ones the existing prose verbs use". Three of the five listed refusals are new, not reused: no existing prose verb refuses on a block being a heading, none refuses on a block carrying no citations, and citation resolution is deliberately not checked at all — prose.rs's module doc says creation is "not gated ... citing a nonexistent claim isn't even checked here", and `create`/`revise` refuse only on a missing block, a bad `--level`, a missing `--why`/`--level`, and an empty `--why`. They are workspace-decidable, and they use the same helper; they are not refusals the existing verbs use.

"Added as a variant of the single request shape both front ends already share so the two cannot drift on which missing flag is refused" holds only below the layer where the drift actually is. The shared shape is reached from two per-front-end parameter declarations, and they do not agree about `text`: `ProseParams` (src/mcp.rs:349-378) declares `text: String` with no `#[serde(default)]` and no `Option`, so it is schema-required, while `Command::Prose` (src/main.rs:242-282) declares `text: Option<String>` and the handler (src/main.rs:773-808) falls back to stdin when it is absent. The ack mode has no text. So as written, an MCP `prose --ack P3 --why "..."` is refused by serde before `workspace::refuse` is ever reached — a sixth refusal, not format-level in the claim's sense and not shared — while the CLI equivalent needs no text at all: the two front ends drift on exactly the axis the shared shape is claimed to close. The alternative, relaxing `ProseParams.text` to `Option<String>`, moves the existing create path's missing-text refusal out of serde into hand-written code, which is a behaviour change to the two verbs this design is not otherwise touching, and to a symbol this memo does not declare as a target. Separately, "its refusals are the ones the existing prose verbs already make and no others" is stated over missing flags only: mode selection in both front ends is an if/else-if chain that silently discards the later arms' inputs (src/main.rs:782-808, src/mcp.rs:736-745), so `--ack` alongside `--revise`, `--heading`, `--cites` or `--before` will silently drop one of them unless a refusal is added — the same shape as the `--cites`-silently-discarded-alongside-`--revise` defect this crate already had to fix.

The last clause is right too: an authoring workspace holds no evidence records — they live at `<memo>.evidence.jsonl` beside the rendered memo (F10, F11) — so the verb cannot compute an anchor.

records.prop: An acknowledgement must not enter `render`'s output. Keeping the rendered bytes a function of facts, claims, prose, targets and transplants only — with `acks.jsonl` shipped by the snapshot copy loop but never read by `compose::render` — preserves the determinism the provenance-drift finding rests on, and buys a property that makes the required re-render honest rather than merely tolerable: re-rendering after an ack and nothing else rewrites the snapshot in place, since existing snapshot files are overwritten, while leaving the memo byte-identical. The discharge therefore shows up in version control as a change to the record and no change to the argument, which is exactly what it is.

records.prop: Supersession needs no verb and withdrawal needs one, and both are resolved by log order rather than by timestamp. Supersession is automatic: since suppression is existential over matching keys, a later ack with a different key simply fails to match and a duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing. Withdrawal is a second event, `Unack`, carrying a block id and its own required verbatim `--why`; suppression then requires a key-matching ack appended after the last `Unack` for that block. Naming only the block, rather than a key, is sufficient because a key-mismatched ack is already void. Resolving by position in an append-only log written one line per event, rather than by comparing timestamps, keeps the whole acknowledgement mechanism free of clock comparisons. Withdrawal has to exist: without it, an author who acknowledged in error and cannot yet rewrite the paragraph would have no honest act available — which is precisely the defect this design was written to remove, reproduced one level up.
verdicts: `workspace::append_jsonl` writes exactly one line per event to an append-only file and `read_jsonl` returns them in file order, so "later than the last Unack" is decidable by position without any timestamp comparison — which is what the proposition rests on. Supersession-by-existential-match and the sufficiency of naming only the block follow from the key being an equality test that a mismatched ack simply fails.

"A duplicate ack for the same key changes nothing" is true of suppression and false of the output the design mandates. C8 puts only (block id, text, cite list, cited-claim digests) in the key; `--why` and the timestamp are recorded and unkeyed. Since every key component is fixed by the state the check recomputes, same-key duplicates are the only multiplicity reachable at suppression time — and C7 requires the collapsed bullet to carry, per acknowledged block, one acknowledgement timestamp and one `--why` verbatim. An author who acknowledges the same unchanged block twice with different reasons therefore leaves the report with two candidate reasons and two candidate timestamps and no stated rule for choosing, so two workspaces in identical states can print different bullets. The design needs one sentence — latest matching ack wins, or all matching acks print — and C14 currently reads as though the question does not arise.

The source facts are all correct: `snapshot::write` copies under `if src.exists()` and never removes, `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is an explicit enumeration so a build predating an acks entry refreshes prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl while never touching acks.jsonl, and the ack's other invalidators (block text, cite list, cited claim propositions) all travel in prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl, which every build ships and rewrites. The clause I cannot let stand as written is the reason given for removing `Unack`: "`snapshot::write` copies and never removes, so a snapshot's ack log is the most recent copy any build made of it rather than the workspace's log as of the last render." C4 of this same ledger states that this design **must** change exactly that — "The writer must reconcile — deleting a snapshot file absent from the workspace". Once C4's reconciliation lands, an appended `Unack` travels in the same rewritten acks.jsonl as every other ack and is no more droppable than they are for any current build; the asymmetry survives only via the *older-build* clause, which C14 also states but subordinates. So the proposition holds under a condition it does not state — that the reader is an older build — and its leading premise is one the memo elsewhere undertakes to falsify.

The mechanism the second consideration rests on is exact: `snapshot::write` iterates only SNAPSHOT_FILES, so a build predating an acks.jsonl entry refreshes prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl and leaves the ack log at whatever the last knowing render wrote — an Unack appended after that render never travels while the ack it cancelled, already in the snapshot, does. The clause about withdrawal having been designed in and then removed is about this memo's own drafting and is not settleable from source; nothing in the tree contradicts it.

The two source-anchored premises hold. Monotonicity: `append_jsonl` (workspace.rs:451-456) opens with `create(true).append(true)` and only writes a line, and no production code path in src/ removes or truncates a workspace log — every `fs::remove` is in a `#[cfg(test)]` region over a temp-dir scratch path. The `Unack` loss scenario is exactly what `snapshot::write` (snapshot.rs:135-146) implies: it copies only names in SNAPSHOT_FILES and never deletes, so a build predating the entry leaves a snapshot's ack log at whatever the last knowing render wrote — a later withdrawal would be invisible while the acknowledgement it cancelled survived. That a repaired paragraph voids its ack follows from the key including text and cite-list, which `prose_after_proof`'s own pair-keying (checks.rs:518-556) shows is the same quantity the trigger tracks. The rest — that matching is existential over keys, and the asymmetry argument for declining the verb — are design stipulations, coherent given those premises.

records.prop: The implementation surface is four declared modification targets plus a new `acks` module, and the censuses bound the blast radius. `prose_after_proof` gains an acks input and returns the listed and acknowledged partitions rather than one list; it has exactly one production call site, in `lib.rs`, the other 31 occurrences being its own definition, eighteen unit-test calls in `checks.rs` and doc-comment or test-name references. `prose_revised_since_proof` on `Findings` gains a sibling field for the acknowledged partition, touching five sites in three files. `SNAPSHOT_FILES` grows from nine entries to ten, touching one file. `NON_COVERAGE` gains entries, touching one file. No other symbol in the worktree needs to change.
verdicts: C15's last sentence — "No other symbol in the worktree needs to change" — is false on this design's own terms, and the symbols it misses are uncensused. C12 specifies the verb as "a variant of the single request shape both front ends already share". That shape is `prose::ProseRequest` (src/prose.rs:211), a three-variant enum consumed by an exhaustive `match` in `prose::dispatch` (src/prose.rs:228-244). Adding a variant therefore forces edits to at least: `ProseRequest`; `prose::dispatch`; `ProseOutcome` (src/prose.rs:216, two variants — an ack is neither `Revised` nor `Created`) and the two exhaustive matches over it at src/main.rs:811-822 and src/mcp.rs:745-749; the clap variant `Command::Prose { text, heading, level, cites, before, revise, why }` and its mode-selection chain at src/main.rs:773-810; and `ProseParams` plus the mode-selection chain and `#[tool(description=...)]` string at src/mcp.rs:735-744. C14 compounds it: `Unack` is a second event needing a second mode through the same chain. None of these seven-plus symbols is among the four declared modification targets (`prose_after_proof`, `prose_revised_since_proof`, `SNAPSHOT_FILES`, `NON_COVERAGE`), none is inside the proposed new `acks` module, and none is censused by F11 — so the memo's own sentence "the censuses bound the blast radius" does not hold for the front-end half of the change. The census I ran (grep `ProseRequest`, whole worktree) names the sites; the memo's ledger names none of them.

One census is wrong. `prose_after_proof` occurs 33 times across src/ and tests/ — one production call site plus **32** other occurrences, not 31 (src/checks.rs 24, src/lib.rs 3, src/report.rs 2, tests/authoring_cli.rs 3, tests/check_cli.rs 1); restricting to src/ gives 29, i.e. one plus 28. No scoping I could find yields 31. Everything else holds: the sole production call is lib.rs:201 (lib.rs:173 and :181 are comments), exactly 18 of the checks.rs occurrences are unit-test calls, `prose_revised_since_proof` occurs at exactly five sites in three files, `SNAPSHOT_FILES` is `[&str; 9]` and appears only in src/snapshot.rs, and `NON_COVERAGE` appears only in src/report.rs. "No other symbol in the worktree needs to change" is a statement about unwritten code and was not independently established.

The enumeration "seven declared modification targets plus a new `acks` module" is short by at least two symbols the verb C12 specifies cannot be built without changing, and neither is reachable from any census in this memo. `ProseParams` (src/mcp.rs:349-378) has no `ack` field; adding the MCP half of `prose --ack <id> --why <text>` means adding one, with its JsonSchema description — a change to the published tool schema. `Command::Prose` (src/main.rs:242-282) has no `--ack` flag; adding the CLI half means adding one. records.prop: This design knowingly breaks both halves of TET-30's C11 sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes": a tenth file ships, and a new event schema exists. The price is bounded and should be stated rather than absorbed. `check` always prints the binary that produced a report, on the stated ground that a report which does not name its build cannot be disbelieved, so two reports disagreeing about one memo's residue can be attributed to their checkers — which is sufficient for the only divergence this change can produce, an older build over-reporting an entry a newer one suppresses. It is not sufficient to tell the reader of a single old report that an acknowledgement exists at all; what covers that is the acknowledgement log itself, which the snapshot ships beside the memo and which is readable without any tetel build.
verdicts: The tetel-side halves are exact: `report::render` prints "checked by {build}" on every path including the no-rows path, its doc comment gives precisely the stated ground ("A report that does not name its build cannot be disbelieved", echoed in buildid.rs: "A verdict that names its checker can be disbelieved; one that does not, cannot"), and a jsonl log shipped in the snapshot is readable without any tetel build. What this pass could not establish is the attribution: a grep of docs/design/tet30-prose-revised-since-grounding.md confirms the sentence "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes" occurs there exactly once, but I retrieved only the match count and did not open the surrounding text, so that the sentence belongs to that memo's C11 is unverified here.

`report::render`'s doc states the build "is *always* printed, including on the no-rows path, because the whole point is that two outputs which disagree can be told apart by their checker. A report that does not name its build cannot be disbelieved" — exactly the stated ground the proposition cites, and it covers attributing two divergent reports to their checkers without telling a single old report's reader that an ack exists. The tenth-file and new-schema price is real given SNAPSHOT_FILES is nine entries today (F2) and ProseEvent admits only Create/Revise (F3, F9).

C16's enumeration of cross-build divergence is incomplete, and the missing member is created by this memo's own C11. C16 asserts the build line is "sufficient for the only divergence this change can produce, an older build over-reporting an entry a newer one suppresses". C11 requires an unreadable acks.jsonl to redden by gaining a disjunct in machine_check_failed. Those two together produce a second divergence class the claim does not admit: on a snapshot whose acks.jsonl holds one malformed line, a build carrying the new disjunct exits 1 on the machine partition while a build predating the SNAPSHOT_FILES entry never opens the file and runs clean. F1 witnesses each step — src/lib.rs:132-211 names every snapshot input literally with no directory enumeration; src/snapshot.rs:185-205 shows snapshot::check only re-renders and imposes no completeness requirement; src/workspace.rs:459-471 shows read_jsonl returns Ok(empty) only for NotFound and Err for any parse failure or other IO error; src/report.rs:181-201 shows machine_check_failed gating the whole machine partition and the exit status. The corrupt state is reachable without any tooling, and the memo's own C17 line 3 and C21 concede a hand-edited snapshot ack log is invisible to drift, so nothing else reports it first.

What survives: "sufficient" — the build line does let a reader attribute a red/green disagreement as readily as an over-reported entry. What does not survive is "the only divergence". The condition C16 needs and does not state is that the snapshot's acks.jsonl is readable; outside it, the divergence is not an extra human-owed line but a build-dependent pass/fail, which the cost paragraph this claim backs ("What changes, and what it costs", cites C16/C8/C4) does not price. Either narrow the clause to divergences in the residue's human-owed entries and price the machine-partition one separately, or state that the ack log's readability is a precondition of the bounded-cost argument.

Both quoted grounds are verbatim. TET-30's C11 row (docs/design/tet30-prose-revised-since-grounding.md:104) does contain "Nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes", so both halves are what this design breaks. report::render takes `build` and prints "checked by {build}" on the no-rows path and at the end of every normal report, with the doc comment stating exactly the ground the claim gives it — "A report that does not name its build cannot be disbelieved" — which is what lets either divergence be attributed to its checker while leaving the single-old-report reader uncovered.

The two divergence kinds are correctly typed. The ordinary one is human-owed: prose_revised_since_proof is a Findings field absent from machine_check_failed's explicit disjunction and from total_failures' sum, so an older build over-reporting one entry costs exactly one human-owed line. The sharper one is red-versus-green because SNAPSHOT_FILES is a closed nine-entry manifest, so a build predating the tenth entry never opens acks.jsonl and cannot reach any disjunct over it.

records.prop: Two entries are owed in `NON_COVERAGE`, by the list's own stated standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed. First: that an acknowledgement records only that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and that nothing verifies the reading happened or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — the tool's silence after an ack is the author's assertion, not the tool's finding. Second: that an acknowledgement minted after the last `render --out` is not in the snapshot the check reads, so it does not suppress anything until the memo is re-rendered. Both are static general statements, which is the only form entries in this constant can take.
verdicts: NON_COVERAGE's own comments state both halves of the standard invoked — "a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed" and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here" — and also state the form constraint: "This can only ever be the general statement — every string in this list is static and none is per-search". Both proposed entries are static general statements of that form, and the second is consistent with the check reading only the shipped snapshot.

The stated standard is in the constant verbatim: "Printed rather than left implicit, because a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed", and "A deliberate exclusion earns its own line, by the same standard as every other entry here." The form constraint is also stated: "This can only ever be the general statement — every string in this list is static and none is per-search", and every element of `NON_COVERAGE` is indeed a `&'static str`. All three proposed entries are static general statements of that shape, and none duplicates an existing entry.

records.prop: Per-citation attribution is folded into the acknowledgement only as far as it honestly can be, which is not far. `NON_COVERAGE`'s last entry already states that whether a block's wording was ever examined against an earlier-settled co-citation is never answered by any listing, and the acknowledgement does not answer it either: the ack is per block, its key merely records every cited claim's digest, and the only place a per-citation judgement can appear is inside the author's verbatim `--why`, which the tool must not parse. The design's contribution is therefore to print the block's cited claim ids beside that verbatim reason in the acknowledged bullet, so a reader can pair the author's own words to the citations, and to leave the non-coverage entry standing.
verdicts: The last entry of NON_COVERAGE is the co-citation one, and it ends in the words the proposition attributes to it: "whether the wording was ever actually examined against the earlier-settled claim is never answered by any listing here". A per-block key carrying every cited claim's digest answers no per-citation question, so leaving that entry standing and printing the cited ids beside the verbatim reason is the whole of the contribution, as stated.

records.prop: The acknowledgement log is re-homeable into TET-36's obligation ledger without rewriting a single event, because no field in it is specific to this residue. It records a block id, the block's text and citation list, a digest per cited claim, a reason and a timestamp; it records none of the quantities `prose_after_proof` derives — not the anchor, not any claim's first proof, not the block timestamp, not whether the block was listed. A general ledger consuming these as discharge records for one obligation class therefore needs the events as they stand and a rule that reads them, which is a re-homing rather than a rework.
verdicts: The quantities prose_after_proof derives are exactly the anchor, each claim's first-proof timestamp, the block's first-appearance timestamp and the listed/not-listed decision (checks.rs:414-557), and none of them appears in the event schema C8 specifies — that schema is block id, text, cite list, per-claim digest, reason, timestamp, all of which are inputs or authorial content. The re-homing conclusion is a statement about TET-36's unwritten ledger and was not independently checked, but nothing in the schema contradicts it.

The quantities `prose_after_proof` derives are the per-claim first proof, the per-block anchor (`cited.iter().map(...).max()`), the block timestamp, and the listed/not-listed decision — none of which appears among the five fields C8 defines plus the timestamp. Every field the ack records (block id, text, cite list, digest per cited claim, reason, time) is a generic discharge record, so re-homing it needs a new consuming rule rather than an event rewrite.

records.prop: This design neither settles nor depends on TET-61's separate question of warning an author at `prose --revise` time. It changes only the economics of that question: today such a warning could name no act, since the workspace verbs are create and revise and neither discharges anything, whereas afterwards it could name the ack verb. Whether the warning is worth building remains a measurement question this memo does not answer.
verdicts: prose.rs holds exactly two acts — `create` and `revise` (ProseEvent has only Create and Revise; ProseRequest's three modes dispatch to those two) — and neither writes anything a check consults as a discharge, so a warning raised at `prose --revise` time today could name no act. The rest of the proposition disclaims settling the measurement question.

The workspace prose verbs are exactly create (paragraph/heading) and revise, in both front ends — `ProseRequest` has three variants covering those two acts and nothing else (F3), so today a revise-time warning could name no discharging act. The remainder of the proposition is a statement about what this memo does not settle, which I take at face value.
